nytimes.com.title: Police in India Detain Hundreds Rallying Against ‘Vote Theft’
nytimes.com.text:
Police in India’s capital city on Friday detained hundreds of protesters calling for the resignation of the country’s election chief, with authorities barricading roads and restricting mobile internet access.
The protest in New Delhi was one of several planned against a contentious revision of the country’s voter rolls that have led to more than 130 million names being dropped across the country. Opposition groups accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi of ‘vote theft’ — claiming that his party is using the election commission to try and rig the rolls in its favor.
Officials from Mr. Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party have denied the allegations, saying the election commission is an independent institution and the rolls are being updated to weed out what they call “infiltrators.”
India’s largest opposition coalition, called the I.N.D.I.A. bloc, announced nationwide protests starting on Friday, and said they would march on the election commission next Tuesday. The Cockroach Janta Party, a youth pressure group whose earlier protests forced the education minister to quit over an exam leak scandal, led demonstrations in Mumbai later in the day.
In Mumbai, the scenes were more joyful as thousands of people, clapping, singing and waving Indian flags, gathered near Shivaji Park, the city’s largest.
Smaller groups and student unions have also joined in the calls for action, with protests expected around the country on Friday, a national holiday.

nytimes.com.title: Indian Pilot Stabbed on FlyDubai Flight Recalls Sudden Attack
nytimes.com.text:
The Indian pilot who was attacked during a FlyDubai flight this week said on Friday that he opened the cockpit door despite grievous injuries, allowing passengers and crew members to overpower the co-pilot who had assailed him.
“I was fighting for my life,” Capt. Smit Machchhar said on a video call from his hospital bed with Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, in his first public remarks since the attack. Video of their conversation was released by the Indian government.
“I was so badly hurt that I had fallen to the ground,” said Captain Machchhar. “But I knew I had to act,” he added. “I could feel the aircraft was going down.”
The attack, on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying about 170 passengers, sent the aircraft into a terrifying plunge. Israeli officials have said the co-pilot appeared to have tried to crash the plane after stabbing Captain Machchhar, although investigators are still trying to understand the assailant’s motives and how the attack unfolded. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination” but did not elaborate.
Passengers were able to overpower the attacker, while two people aboard with flying experience helped land the plane in Saudi Arabia.
Captain Machchhar, who said he had 17 years of flying experience, including 11 as a captain, said he knew instinctively what was happening to the aircraft, even as he lay injured on the cockpit floor. The Boeing 737 Max 8 he was flying plummeted more than 16,000 feet in 30 seconds during the attack.
Captain Machchhar told Mr. Modi that he recalled telling himself: “Smit, this is the last push, just do it. The door is right there.”
“I was doing it to save myself,” he said, “but I also knew I couldn’t let all of them die.”
Captain Machchhar, who was hospitalized in Saudi Arabia then transferred to the United Arab Emirates, told Mr. Modi that he was receiving good medical care.
The episode has made him a hero in India.
“Your courage and presence of mind — you made a decision within a fraction of a second, and saved so many lives,” Mr. Modi told the captain during their conversation. “You have made the entire country proud.”
Mr. Modi’s office put out the video of the split-screen conversation on a day of nationwide protests in India, including in the capital, New Delhi. Protesters are demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election officer for trying to rig voter rolls in the favor of Mr. Modi’s party.
Captain Machchhar grew up in Mumbai and entered aviation almost by accident after attending a seminar on flying. He later became a captain and a trainer of aspiring pilots. In a podcast interview last year, he described flying as something he felt “blessed” to do and emphasized the importance of pilots being rested and prepared to perform under pressure.
Suhasini Raj contributed reporting.

cnn.com.title: Trump is expected to name Jay Clayton as AI czar
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump is expected to pick Jay Clayton to be the White House’s new czar of artificial intelligence, two sources familiar with the discussion told CNN. The president could announce his decision about Clayton, who is director of national intelligence, as early as Friday, one of the sources said. Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. Trump gathered several AI and technology CEOs at the White House on Tuesday for a meeting that culminated in the signing of a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models. Trump previously told Axios that Clayton would be a good AI czar. CBS News first reported that Clayton was the frontrunner for the position. A White House official told CNN, “Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation.” Clayton, who previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during the majority of Trump’s first term, is expected to remain in his role as director of national intelligence, the sources said. He was confirmed by the Senate in July to lead the US intelligence community. Clayton succeeded Bill Pulte, a controversial housing executive with no national security experience whom Trump installed as acting director for a 40-day tenure. When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer” and that it’s “not only an opportunity but a threat.” “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now co-chairs the president’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Sacks has continued to have considerable influence on the president when it comes to AI issues. On Tuesday, Trump told reporters that he was “very close to making a decision,” regarding his pick for the role. “I’ll be naming one, I’d say, over the next three or four days.” Trump added that he first wanted to check with “the companies” as well as House GOP leadership in Congress before making his decision. The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.”

cnn.com.title: US pressures Europe to release diesel reserves ‘immediately’ to tame prices
cnn.com.text: European officials are holding crisis talks as the United States piles pressure on the region to tap into its emergency stocks of diesel to cool surging prices – or face a possible ban on US exports of the fuel. European officials discussed measures to tackle high diesel prices on Friday, the European Commission said in a statement, while France said it would chair a meeting of G7 leaders on the “global energy situation” later in the day. The veiled ultimatum from the US administration marks an escalation in pressure on Europe as President Donald Trump attempts to bring down US fuel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections Diesel is the workhorse fuel for the global economy, powering trucks, tractors, freight trains and other commercial vehicles. The US is the world’s largest exporter of the fuel and US President Donald Trump has touted a ban on diesel exports as a way to boost domestic supplies – and, in turn, bring down prices. A US diesel export ban would hit Europe – a net-importer of the fuel – hard, analysts told CNN. Last year, the US supplied around 13% of the combined 2.3 million barrels Europe, the United Kingdom and Turkey imported every day, according to data from market intelligence firm Energy Aspects. But tapping into its emergency reserves risks leaving Europe exposed should supply disruptions from the war in the Middle East and Ukraine continue. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged European countries on Thursday to release diesel from its stockpiles “immediately,” writing in a post on X that “American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage.” US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who has previously expressed reservations about a ban on US diesel exports, told Fox News on Thursday that the US is “absolutely” going to ask Europe to release diesel from its strategic reserves. “This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go into harvest season, and we go into winter heating oil season. Now is the time to bring more diesel to the market,” he said. The US-Iran war – now in its eight month – has disrupted flows of crude and refined oil products from the Middle East. While Europe is not currently grappling with outright shortages, global supplies are tight and prices have soared. US diesel prices have also shot up since the start of the war and, last month, topped $6 a gallon for the first time, according to data from AAA. The average price stood at $6.40 a gallon on Friday morning. Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, a spokesperson for the European Commission, told reporters at a briefing on Thursday that member states were in “very close contact” on the issue of diesel supply and that it was also in contact with the US administration. “I can assure you that lots of phone calls, lots of meetings are taking place at this point,” she said. ‘Grappling and fighting’ A US ban would see Europeans “paying an even higher premium” for (imported) diesel… because it will be competing against other regions that are net importers like Latin America,” said Richard Bronze, Energy Aspects’ co-founder. The US may be one of several suppliers to Europe, he added, but Washington is such a critical supplier to the international market that a ban of its exports would see countries “grappling and fighting over what remains.” Europe’s benchmark diesel prices have more than doubled since the start of the US-Iran war in late February, according to Intercontinental Exchange data. Worsening the picture is a ban on diesel exports from Russia – which Moscow recently extended until the end of October – following Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries. As are indications from China that it may tighten restrictions on its oil product exports, said Bronze. EU member states are required to hold oil stocks equal to 90 days of net imports, but the Commission does not specify how those stocks should be divided between crude oil, jet fuel, kerosene and diesel. Matt Stanley, head of market engagement at Kpler, highlighted Europe’s dilemma and the risks posed by dipping into emergency reserves in an uncertain geopolitical environment. “If the underlying disruption continues, you cannot keep drawing inventories indefinitely without eventually creating a much bigger supply problem,” he told CNN. In March, member countries of the International Energy Agency agreed to release 400 million barrels of oil into the global market – the largest release of emergency oil stocks in history – in response to the US-Iran war. But the US argues that Europe has not fulfilled its side of the bargain. Bronze, at Energy Aspects, said that the European Union has released less than 8% of the 64 million barrels of oil products – including diesel – that it pledged in the spring.

cnn.com.title: Radio signal detected from exoplanet for the first time
cnn.com.text: Astronomers say they have directly detected the first-ever radio emission from a planet outside the solar system. The signal, however, is evidence of a colossal magnetic field — not intelligent life. “I know radio signals are associated with searches for extraterrestrial intelligence,” said Edo Berger, a professor of astronomy at Harvard University. “But this is something very different.” The discovery, described in a new paper awaiting publication in a peer-reviewed journal, traces repeating radio bursts that appear to come from the exoplanet Beta Pictoris b, located 63 light-years from Earth — a short distance, astronomically speaking. The gas giant, about 12 times the mass of Jupiter, is one of three planets orbiting a young star that is 1.75 times as massive as the sun. Processes associated with the planet’s magnetic field produce the radio emission, according to Berger, a researcher at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Specifically, the detection involves auroras similar to Earth’s northern lights — the spectacular displays sparked by magnetic storms involving charged particles from the sun. “In order to see radio waves that extend all the way to the frequencies that we observed, you need an incredibly strong magnetic field,” added Berger, a coauthor of the paper posted September 15 to the preprint platform ArXiv. Not all planets have a magnetic field. Those that have one benefit from a natural shield that deflects disruptive energy. Earth’s magnetic field, for example, protects our atmosphere from being stripped away by solar wind, a continuous outflow of plasma that contains charged particles like protons and electrons. “The magnetic field on this planet is at least 200 times stronger than the magnetic field of Jupiter,” Berger said, referring to Beta Pictoris b. Jupiter’s magnetic field, according to NASA, is powerful enough to generate a magnetosphere — the region of space influenced by the magnetic field — that ranks as the largest structure in our solar system, stretching up to 2 million miles (3 million kilometers) toward the sun. Jupiter’s field also creates striking auroras, when electrically charged particles spewed from volcanoes on its moon Io become trapped around the field’s poles. As the gas giant rotates, the charged particles emit a glow but also a radio signal. “As these very high-energy particles are spiraling inside the magnetic field, along with the aurora they also produce radio waves,” Berger said. Astronomers call this type of signal an auroral radio emission. The phenomenon has been previously observed from Jupiter, Saturn and the sun, as well as stars outside the solar system and cool objects known as brown dwarfs — an intermediate between a star and a planet. This type of signal is what Berger and his colleagues detected from Beta Pictoris b, which ultimately points to the presence of an intense magnetic field that’s causing auroras and the radio emission. Magnetic fields have implications for the structure of exoplanets and their atmospheres, according to Berger. “Radio observations can give us a completely new view on planets beyond our system,” he said. A well-studied star system There had been hints of radio emissions from exoplanets before, but none had been confirmed, largely because it couldn’t be ruled out that the source was actually the host star, said Joseph Callingham, an associate professor at the Anton Pannekoek Institute for Astronomy of the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands. “What is unique for this study is that they localise the emission to the planet itself, separate from the star,” Callingham, who was not involved in the new research, wrote in an email. The Beta Pictoris system is astronomically very young at about 23 million years old compared with our own solar system’s age of 4.5 billion years. Beta Pictoris b — the planet from which the radio signal potentially originates — was discovered in 2008. Two additional planets, Beta Pictoris c and Beta Pictoris d, were discovered in 2019 and 2026, respectively. The planetary system is among the most studied in our galaxy, and its star is known to host 30 orbiting comets and a giant disk of dust and debris, which NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope photographed in detail in 2015. Some of the debris swirling in the rotating disk is a remnant from planetary formation. The researchers used MeerKAT, an array of 64 radio telescope dishes in South Africa, to detect the signal, but they were highly surprised to see it coming from such a well-observed set of celestial bodies, Berger said. “My graduate student Kevin was going through the data. He came into my office one day with the detection and he said, ‘I don’t think you’re going to believe this,’” Berger recalled, referring to lead study author Kevin Ortiz Ceballos, a doctoral researcher at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “This was really unexpected for us. We were doing the survey as a bit of a fishing expedition, knowing that we would only detect sources if the magnetic field was incredibly strong.” The surprise stems from the fact that astronomers had assumed, according to Berger, that if exoplanets have magnetic fields, they should look roughly like Jupiter’s, and therefore their radio emissions would be at lower frequencies than what he and his colleagues found. Detecting the signal was the result of “going against the perceived wisdom in the field,” he said. However, the researchers noted the report has not yet undergone peer review, the process in which independent experts assess a research paper before publication in a scientific journal. The review is underway and will be completed over the next few months. Berger said he is confident about the quality of the detection. The research team pinpointed the radio emission’s source as Beta Pictoris b, ruling out an initial suspicion that it could be coming from the star instead. “We recorded it multiple times, at multiple frequencies. It’s there every single time,” he said. Cautious enthusiasm for radio signal detection Scientists who were not involved with the new research urged caution when interpreting the findings. If the discovery holds up under the scrutiny of peer review, it would represent an incredibly exciting and key step forward in understanding the behavior of worlds beyond our solar system, according to Jonathan Nichols, a professor in planetary auroras at the University of Leicester in England. “Auroral radio emissions are important because they allow us to understand how an object interacts with its local space environment,” he wrote in an email. “They allow us to infer properties of the planet that we cannot otherwise measure,” Nichols explained, referring to auroras, “and, importantly, they enable us to test theories and ideas developed for our own solar system in more extreme conditions.” If confirmed, the results would show that exoplanets can have much stronger magnetic fields than expected, which would be a crucial learning, according to Callingham of the University of Amsterdam. The authors have requested more telescope time to further study Beta Pictoris b and perhaps unlock some of its puzzles, such as why the planet’s magnetic field is so strong. “I think that’s going to be a question that occupies people for a while,” Berger said.

cnn.com.title: Students and police clash as France’s government struggles to calm student tensions
cnn.com.text: Students fought running battles with police and several schools were ablaze Friday as a new day of violence gripped France with no end in sight to protests that have rocked the country. The government announced more than 400 schools would be closed on Friday as it scrambled to calm tensions after days of demonstrations that have seen hundreds of teenagers taken into custody. Young people in Strasbourg, eastern France, were building barricades in tear gas-clouded streets, while more peaceful protests were underway in Lyon and other cities Friday. The protestors say France’s education sector is under-resourced and overstretched. Students complain that absent teachers aren’t being replaced and say schools are in a state of serious disrepair. “We’ve moved from student protests to a question of public order,” Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said Friday morning, adding he feared the unrest would carry on through the weekend. Nationwide union-led protests in support of the high schoolers are planned for Tuesday. With no obvious off-ramp for the protests and tensions rising as the violence continues, the government is scrambling to contain the situation outside high schools. French Education Minister Édouard Geffray will meet with representatives of students, parents and staff on Friday, but given the highly localized nature of the protests, this may not provide a quick resolution. Authorities in several parts of the country banned gatherings around the schools that were closed Friday, but the measure appears to have had little effect. Speaking to radio station RTL, Darmanin proposed making parents pay for the damage incurred by students, an idea shot down as “absurd” by the far-left France Unbowed party, whose politicians have drawn criticism for rallying with students. On Thursday, government officials called on parents to prevent their children from taking part in violent protests. Many of the protests at high schools are peaceful, but the images of arson and strong-arm police tactics are dominating the public debate in France. High schools in poorer suburbs of cities across the country have been at the center of the ongoing tensions with police. As of Friday morning, some 2,000 people had been taken into custody over the student protests, 90% of them adolescents, according to the justice ministry. Two students suffered serious injuries after allegedly being struck by crowd-control rounds fired by police. In a post on X on Thursday, the Paris police prefecture said that its officers had been “challenged by individuals determined to clash” during Thursday’s protests. Agathe Foucault, a spokesperson for French police, told CNN affiliate BFMTV on Friday that officers “are required to use force in a necessary and proportionate manner.”

cnn.com.title: States are taking matters into their own hands to fight high gas and diesel prices
cnn.com.text: As the Trump administration deliberates how to fight historically high gas and diesel prices, a growing number of US states are taking matters into their own hands. The state-level action has taken place across the country in recent days and weeks, spanning red states like Texas and Oklahoma, blue states including California and purple states such as Georgia. State officials say they hope to provide temporary relief ahead of the midterms to drivers, farmers and truckers frustrated by sky-high fuel prices, which are driven in large part by the Iran war. Ohio, a major battleground in the elections next month, became the latest to take action on Thursday. Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, signed a bill into law suspending the state’s gasoline and diesel taxes for 90 days beginning  Sunday. Both gubernatorial candidates – Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton – pushed for the tax break. The state actions underscore the pressure on local officials from voters who want lower energy prices. Gas prices are above $4.40 a gallon nationally, and they have never been this high at this time of year — not even in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine. Prices for diesel, the workhorse fuel that powers trucks, tractors, trains and construction vehicles, hit all-time highs last month but has since backed away a bit. Analysts say the states’ moves could help American consumers and businesses on the margin, but none of the actions will drastically change the reality of high prices. The main problem is that the Iran war, the Russia-Ukraine conflict and export restrictions in China have spurred a global shortage of refining. “States are taking actions where they have control, but they can’t control the events in the Middle East and Russia – and those events are much bigger drivers of prices than temporary relief steps states can offer,” said Andy Lipow, president of consulting firm Lipow Oil Associates. “If you want to lower prices, end the Iran conflict.” Oil exports out of the Middle East have raced back to life in recent weeks, thanks in part to US military escorts. And President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that the war will end soon and that gas prices will plummet shortly after. But elected officials, particularly Republicans, are growing increasingly antsy to demonstrate they are doing something as the midterm elections near. States suspending gas taxes Ohio’s bill will temporarily suspend its gas and diesel fuel taxes of 38.5 cents a gallon and 47 cents a gallon, respectively. The measure is estimated to save drivers a total of $725 million over the next three months. Other states have also taken various actions to give drivers some tax relief. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, a Republican, renewed a pause on Wednesday for another month to give “Hoosier families additional breathing room to make ends meet while protecting funding for state and local infrastructure projects,” according to a statement from the governor’s office. Braun first suspended gasoline taxes in the spring. And in Georgia, Republican Gov. Brian Kemp declared a state of emergency  Monday, suspending the taxes on gas and diesel fuel for a month. Kemp also signed legislation in the spring temporarily pausing the levies, which resumed in early June. Kentucky and Illinois, which both have Democratic governors, also took measures earlier this year to temporarily lighten gas levies. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear temporarily reduced gas taxes by 10 cents in the spring and blocked a small increase in the tax that would have kicked in on July 1. And in June, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker delayed a scheduled 1.3-cent increase in the gas tax for six months. A few congressional lawmakers from both parties have also floated suspending the federal gas tax of 18.4 cents, though their efforts did not go far on Capitol Hill. Although suspending state gas taxes is a good talking point for politicians, fuel and policy analysts say they are not that effective. Drivers typically receive only between 60% and 80% of the savings from gas tax holidays, with the rest captured by gas stations and other players in the supply chain, said Alex Arnon, director of policy analysis at Penn Wharton Budget Model, an initiative that has studied the impact of gas tax suspensions. In the current highly uncertain environment, Arnon expects savings will be on the lower end for drivers. “Everybody along the supply chain has both an incentive and more opportunity to siphon off a little bit of the savings from that gas tax holiday,” he said. Also, reducing gas taxes only spurs demand without increasing supply, which can end up raising prices, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “The market is telling you it’s in distress, something’s wrong,” he told CNN. “The way to respond to that shouldn’t be, ‘Oh, hey, let’s cut the price so Americans don’t have to make tough decisions.’” Help for truckers To help truckers cope with the diesel spike, Texas, Alabama, Oklahoma, Nebraska and other states have taken steps to boost red-dyed diesel. Red-dyed diesel is the same as regular diesel. It’s just untaxed and dyed to classify it for off-road use only, such as farming. By allowing red-dyed diesel to be used on highways, state officials can save truckers some money. But the savings are relatively modest. “It’s all the same diesel,” Lipow said. “They’re hoping to save truckers and farmers some money that can ultimately be passed through to consumers.” Another frequent step state officials take to help lower fuel costs is allowing refineries to switch to cheaper winter-blend fuel earlier than usual. California and Michigan have both taken this measure in recent months. Most states east of the Rocky Mountains have already switched over to the cheaper winter fuel. The move can help save drivers in California about 25 cents a gallon, Lipow said, though he noted the famously expensive state is grappling with refinery outages that could offset the savings.

cnn.com.title: Flávio Bolsonaro inherited his father’s right-wing movement. Can he win Brazil’s presidency?
cnn.com.text: Standing atop a truck equipped with loudspeakers on Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach, Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his campaign, addressing the inevitable comparison with the man whose footsteps he is trying to follow. “I know you are looking at me right now and thinking of someone,” he told thousands of supporters gathered on August 16 in the city where his political career began. “I know I look like him, but it is difficult to compare Pelé’s son to Pelé.” The reference to Brazil’s most famous soccer player drew laughter, but it captured the challenge at the heart of Bolsonaro’s presidential candidacy: how to capitalize on his similarities with his father, ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, while convincing voters that a different Bolsonaro can inherit the movement built around him. The physical resemblance is obvious. Flávio shares his father’s light-colored eyes, dark hair, defined features and some of his gestures when speaking. But as he campaigns to succeed the man who transformed Brazil’s right, he has struggled to connect with voters in the same way his father did. That is why, for much of the rally, escaping Jair Bolsonaro’s shadow did not even seem to be the goal. Flávio played recordings of the former president, promised to continue his legacy and said he had “humbly” accepted the mission his father had entrusted to him. Convicted of more than 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after his 2022 electoral defeat, Jair Bolsonaro has entrusted Flávio with continuing his legacy, while maintaining his innocence and hoping that his son’s path to the presidential palace could also lead to his own freedom. At 45, Flávio now faces a task that even his father could not accomplish: defeating Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who, at nearly 81, is seeking a fourth and likely final term. But just days before the first round, both candidates face controversies — corruption allegations, family disputes and a growing institutional crisis involving the Supreme Federal Court and figures across the establishment — while polls show an increasingly close race. A more moderate Bolsonaro? Flávio Nantes Bolsonaro was born in 1981 and is the eldest of Jair Bolsonaro’s five children. A lawyer by profession, he was elected to the Rio de Janeiro state legislature at just 21, long before his father’s rise turned the family name into one of Brazil’s most powerful political brands. Flávio served four terms before reaching the Senate in 2018, the same election in which his father won the presidency. He built his political career in Rio de Janeiro — a state with a long history of organized crime and violence — focusing primarily on hard-line public security policies and defending police officers and other security forces. However, Flávio is perceived as a more moderate and conciliatory Bolsonaro. “During the various crises of Jair Bolsonaro’s government, Flávio appeared to be the family member with some willingness to engage in dialogue,” said Octávio Amorim Neto, a political scientist and professor at the Getulio Vargas Foundation. During his father’s repeated clashes with Congress and the Supreme Federal Court, Flávio cultivated relationships with lawmakers and acted as an informal bridge between his father and the Senate. “Flávio has more tact than his father,” said Gilson Machado, Jair Bolsonaro’s former tourism minister, who has known the former president since the 1990s and Flávio for more than a decade. “He listens more.” Machado, a longtime Bolsonaro ally, was arrested on June 13, 2025 as part of an investigation into whether he had attempted to help Bolsonaro’s former chief of staff and a key witness in the coup-plot case obtain a Portuguese passport and leave Brazil. Machado denied the allegations, and his pretrial detention was revoked that same day, although he still faces restrictions, including the retention of his passport. Machado says he often spends vacations with Flávio in northeastern Brazil and that the senator loves fishing and is passionate about diving. “He is a fearless diver. He goes down to 30 meters (90 feet). I had never seen anything like it,” he said. Machado also offered a glimpse into one of the main differences between father and son: Jair’s more reserved nature compared with Flávio’s more openly affectionate personality. “Bolsonaro has never kissed his children,” he said. “Flávio, on the other hand, kisses his son; he has kissed his father. It is a different style.” But a more moderate personal style does not amount to a more moderate political project. In a 2007 speech, Flávio defended the militias that were expanding their control over parts of Rio at the time, describing them as a “new way of doing police work” that could provide security where the state had failed, in what is widely regarded as one of the most controversial episodes of his career. “As a state lawmaker, he awarded medals to militia members,” Amorim Neto said. “That is one of the major stains on his record, even in the eyes of the right.” A hard-line approach to crime is also a central element of his father’s movement, and Flávio has taken it to the national stage. His campaign puts security front and center, with promises to lower the age of criminal responsibility and toughen the response to violent crime. In March, he called for Brazil’s two largest criminal groups to be designated as terrorist organizations and then traveled to the United States in May to make the request directly to Trump, a measure rejected by Lula and the left, who consider it a threat to Brazilian sovereignty. When the United States announced that the groups would be designated as terrorist organizations, Bolsonaro thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for what he described as a response to his request. The message connects with voters’ main concern: A Quaest poll in August showed that 33% of Brazilians considered violence the country’s main problem, more than twice the percentage who mentioned the economy. A family business After Jair’s conviction left him out of the race, other prominent names emerged to take over the leadership of the right. But the former president pushed to keep the legacy within his own surname. “Politics is the Bolsonaro family business,” Amorim Neto said, and two of the brothers with the longest political careers thus emerged as the leading contenders. Eduardo Bolsonaro had built the strongest international profile among the brothers, cultivating ties with the MAGA movement in the United States and lobbying the Trump administration to pressure Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court over his father’s case. In July 2025, Trump called the case against Jair Bolsonaro a “witch hunt” and announced 50% tariffs on Brazilian imports. Nearly a year later, Brazil’s courts convicted Eduardo of coercion and sentenced him to four years and two months in prison. He remains in the US and risks being arrested if he returns to Brazil. “That effectively left Flávio and his stepmother, former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, as the leading contenders to inherit the family’s political leadership,” Amorim Neto said. For the political scientist, Jair Bolsonaro’s final decision was to favor his own bloodline. “He ended up choosing the eldest son,” he said. But the transition was not easy. Flávio publicly clashed with his stepmother, the former first lady, a powerful figure on Brazil’s right. A dispute over party alliances erupted publicly in June, when Michelle posted videos accusing her stepson of humiliating her politically during a phone call. The rift was particularly delicate because Michelle had built a strong network among conservative women and evangelical Christians, key constituencies for Flávio. Flávio apologized, and the two publicly reconciled in July after weeks of efforts by party leaders to contain the dispute. By September, Michelle had returned to the campaign to support her stepson, asking her network of female supporters to help elect him. Machado told CNN that their relationship is now “as good as it can possibly be.” But the episode exposed a fragmented right and a divided Liberal Party, Bolsonaro’s political base. A scandal that reaches everyone The campaign is also facing other problems. A sweeping corruption investigation into the bankrupt private Brazilian bank, Banco Master, has become a backdrop to the election, reaching politicians across Brazil’s establishment, including the Supreme Federal Court, Lula and Flávio himself. For Flávio, the scandal initially presented an opportunity to revive one of Bolsonarismo’s longest-running battles: its confrontation with the Supreme Federal Court, and particularly with Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw key investigations that ultimately led to Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction. Bolsonaro supporters have since portrayed Moraes as an ally of Lula, although he was not appointed by Lula and does not belong to his party. Investigators uncovered a multimillion-dollar contract between Banco Master and a law firm owned by Moraes’ wife, as well as compromising messages that the bank’s president sent to a contact he had saved under Moraes’ name, according to CNN Brasil. It has not been established that Moraes received or responded to the messages, but the revelations gave Bolsonaro’s campaign enough ammunition to return to one of its most familiar arguments: that the left, and anyone associated with it, is corrupt. “Today we have our No. 10 on the campaign trail,” Machado told CNN. “It is Alexandre de Moraes.” CNN has reached out to Moraes for comment. He has previously denied receiving messages attributed to him, calling the association of his name with them a “false inference” aimed at attacking the Supreme Court. Luciano Da Ros, a political scientist specializing in corruption and Brazil’s judicial system, said that for the Bolsonaro base, interest in Moraes’ possible involvement goes beyond the election. “They hope this will eventually make it possible to overturn the conviction or invalidate his actions in the case on procedural grounds,” he said. But in recent days, the scandal has also reached Flávio. The Supreme Federal Court opened an investigation in July into the senator over alleged corruption and money laundering linked to Banco Master’s financing of “Dark Horse,” a film about Jair Bolsonaro. Flávio has denied wrongdoing and said his ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former owner of Banco Master, were related to the film. Bolsonaro beyond Jair If elected, clashes with the judiciary are unlikely to end. Flávio has promised to seek a broad amnesty for his father and others convicted over the coup attempt, and to use the presidential pardon power if Congress does not act. “That would mean another enormous crisis with the Supreme Federal Court,” Amorim Neto said. A Flávio government is also expected to maintain much of his father’s international alignment, particularly with the US. “Bolsonarismo is intimately linked to MAGA and Trumpism,” Amorim Neto said, arguing that the Bolsonaro family has positioned itself as a follower of Trump’s political movement. But that closeness to Trump has also exposed a contradiction in Bolsonarismo’s nationalist message. “If you are a nationalist or a patriot, first and foremost you put the national interest ahead, not subordination to the leader of the world’s superpower,” Amorim Neto said. “And Brazilian voters see it, they perceive it, and most of them are against it, although Bolsonaro supporters among the electorate back several of Trump’s actions.” That contradiction has emerged repeatedly: in Trump’s tariffs on Brazilian products over the judicial proceedings against Jair Bolsonaro, which Eduardo Bolsonaro had lobbied for; in Flávio’s push for the US to designate Brazil’s largest criminal groups as terrorist organizations; and in debates over US interest in the country’s critical mineral resources. That marks a clear difference between Bolsonaro and Lula: While Flávio has aligned himself with Trump and a growing network of conservative leaders in Latin America, Lula has emphasized Brazil’s sovereignty and interests while deepening ties with China. Putting the power of a legacy to the test Still, those contradictions have not prevented Flávio from consolidating much of the loyal electorate that backed his father. Brazil remains deeply polarized, and the political distribution has changed little since 2022: Flávio draws some of his strongest support from evangelical Christians and higher-income voters, while Lula remains stronger among lower-income Brazilians and Catholics. In a Datafolha poll published in September, Flávio led Lula by nearly two to one among evangelical voters, while Lula maintained a smaller lead among Catholics, 43% to 32%. His emphasis on fighting crime, his anti-left agenda and his confrontations with the Supreme Federal Court and Brazil’s political establishment directly appeal to issues that have mobilized Bolsonaro’s base for years. According to a Quaest poll published in September, nearly all voters who identify as Bolsonaro supporters now back Flávio, suggesting that the movement’s political identity has been transferred even without its founder on the ballot. That inherited support has helped transform a candidacy that initially struggled to escape a turbulent campaign and the shadow of his father into a highly competitive race with Lula. At his first campaign rally in Copacabana, Flávio promised to continue his father’s legacy. And while he may not be a carbon copy of his father, that could be enough to win this October.

cnn.com.title: AI blurs lines in campaign ads: ‘People are seeing things that didn’t happen’
cnn.com.text: Dramatic political attack ads hitting the airwaves this year have shown a Senate candidate driving a bus of undocumented immigrants to a polling place, a governor hopeful grabbing bags stuffed full of cash, and a Republican congressman holding hands with two of his Democratic colleagues in what a narrator described as a “throuple.” None of those compromising situations ever happened — the ads were all generated with artificial intelligence. From January through mid-September, political campaigns and groups had spent more than $16 million on TV ads that disclosed using AI-generated or manipulated images, according to a CNN analysis of ad data. But only about half of states require campaigns to disclose AI use in political ads — and at least $38 million has been spent on ads that strongly appear to include AI imagery despite featuring no disclosure. That includes ads in key midterm races that could sway the balance of power in Congress, such as ads from GOP campaigns and groups showing Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff getting a makeover and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico defacing a Bible. The Ossoff ad didn’t have any disclosure about AI use, while the Talarico ad featured a small disclosure saying that “certain video content” was created with AI. The flood of ads containing lifelike imagery has sparked alarms among lawmakers and voters alike, fearful of being misrepresented and misinformed. Already, the new frontier of AI ads has roiled political campaigns, with some ads being taken off air after complaints by candidates, and a Texas candidate filing a police report alleging that a video depicting her endorsing a list of new taxes violated state law. AI’s use in campaign commercials comes amid public unease with the underlying technology and growing debate among policymakers over how, and whether, to take additional steps to rein it in. A new CNN poll found that about eight in 10 Americans express negative views about the rapid pace of AI development. CNN’s analysis found that Republicans have been quicker to adopt AI in political ads than their Democratic opponents. About 96% of the spending on ads that disclosed AI use came from GOP campaigns or groups. CNN found a handful of ads that appear to skirt state laws about disclosures. In Michigan, a PAC linked to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, a Republican, aired an ad showing Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed laughing at messages saying “Death to America” and “Celebrate 9/11,” and dancing with the left-wing influencer Hasan Piker and other figures. The final seconds of the ad included a disclosure in tiny text and a spoken line acknowledging it was “created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence” — but one Michigan law requires “materially deceptive” ads that aim to influence elections to feature a disclosure “throughout the entirety of the video” that is “clearly visible to and readable by an observer.” In a statement to CNN, El-Sayed campaign spokesman Cole Wozniak said Republicans “are so desperate that they are resorting to cheap AI generated ads filled with falsehoods and bad faith attacks.” The use of AI in political ads ranges from relatively minor changes like animating old family photos to surreal attacks, like one ad that put a Florida governor candidate’s talking head on the body of a fish or another that showed President Donald Trump frying a patty with a congressman’s face on it. While some of the most outlandish ads are obviously AI-generated, experts are worried about less clear cases. The danger is that “people are seeing things that didn’t happen, seeing politicians say things they actually didn’t say,” said Travis Ridout, a political scientist at Washington State University and one of the co-directors of the Wesleyan Media Project, which has studied AI use in political ads. “Even if there’s a disclaimer on there that says this was synthetically generated, oftentimes seeing is believing,” he said. Spending surge To track the growth in spending in AI political ads, CNN analyzed thousands of ads that aired this year and were collected by the tracking service AdImpact. Reporters used AI to extract all text shown on screen in each ad and then manually reviewed those with relevant disclosures. The analysis revealed dozens of ads that disclosed to viewers that they included AI-generated, enhanced or manipulated content. Reporters also reviewed and identified several dozen additional ads that did not disclose using AI but strongly appear to feature AI-generated imagery. Some of those ads were flagged by researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project. Reporters excluded some ads when it was unclear whether they used AI or more traditional graphic effects technology. The analysis found that spending on broadcast TV political ads that clearly featured AI grew from less than $25,000 in January to more than $10 million in the first half of September alone. It’s likely that CNN’s analysis missed some ads that used AI without disclosing it, because the use of the technology is not always obvious. A leading Republican super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, produced an attack ad last month targeting Ossoff that uses AI imagery to mock his campaign spending on hair and makeup. “Thousands on hair and makeup. What a phony,” claims an individual in the ad, which depicts Ossoff receiving cosmetic treatments including a blow dry, eye cucumbers and nail filing. The Georgia Democrat called for the ad to be taken down at a press conference shortly after it was launched, saying it was “deeply troubling to see these deepfake videos used to fabricate political advertising.” An SLF spokesman said it was Ossoff’s record that was “deeply troubling.” Another ad launched last month by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton shows Talarico, his Democratic opponent for US Senate, drawing in a Bible and making statements about religion and gender. The ad features quotes that Talarico said over the years without context — yet they’re spoken not by the actual Talarico, but an AI-generated version of him. “Ken Paxton and his billionaire backers in DC know they can’t rely on facts to win this race — so their only answer is to literally put words in James’ mouth with AI deepfake videos to try and fool Texans,” Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis said in a statement. Paxton’s campaign rejected the criticism. “Our team was diligent in ensuring every piece of the ad was properly sourced and cited,” Paxton spokesperson Madison Cercy said in a statement. “We intend to continue to use all available means to put James Talarico’s radical record in front of Texans.” AI advertising was also a flashpoint in the contentious race to oust GOP Rep. Thomas Massie in Kentucky’s 4th Congressional District earlier this year. One of the outside groups opposing Massie ran ads that featured AI-generated imagery of the congressman walking hand-in-hand with Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar, progressive Democrats vilified by conservatives, but who aligned with Massie on opposition to US military aid for Israel. The ad showed what appeared to be paparazzi photos of the trio dining together, and security footage of them checking into a hotel, as a narrator declared that Massie was “cheating with the squad on the America First movement.” A small text disclosure shown during the ad’s first seconds stated that “this satirical ad was created with artificial intelligence.” After he lost his primary earlier this year, Massie suggested the ad could have contributed to his defeat. “Many older people voted against me because they believed I dated AOC and Omar,” the congressman wrote about the ad in a post on X. “I told AOC I would never do that with Omar!” he joked. Beyond the more contentious examples, many candidates have also turned to AI tools to simply and cheaply produce less controversial campaign content. Rick Jackson, the GOP nominee for Georgia governor, has spent millions this year on ads that include AI animations of family photos and dramatizations of his hardscrabble childhood, making his campaign the top spender on AI ads identified by CNN. (While some of his ads have disclosed using AI, others have not — disclosures are not required in Georgia.) Nathaniel Persily, a Stanford law professor who studies the use of AI in elections, said that deepfake AI ads could end up having the most impact not in prominent statewide races but down-ballot, low-information contests where voters might not take the time to study candidates or fact-check ads they see. “We’ve had Photoshop and attempts to manipulate imagery and lies that politicians have told since the beginning of time,” Persily said. “There’s something about realistic video that makes it more believable to people and has a greater emotional appeal.” States rush in as feds fail to act At least 31 states have passed laws regulating the use of AI content and deepfakes in political advertising, ranging from outright prohibitions to disclosure requirements, according to a tally by the National Conference of State Legislatures. Most of those laws were signed in the last three years, as AI use became more prevalent. Most of the states require some sort of disclosure of AI content or deepfakes in political ads, while three states — Maryland, Minnesota and Texas — have banned some deepfake ads. Minnesota’s and Texas’ prohibitions only apply in specific periods leading up to elections. “This year is a test case to see if those laws are being effective, are they being enforced, whether AI really becomes a major factor in elections,” said Katy Owens Hubler, the director of the NCSL’s elections program. At least a few of the AI-powered ads that have aired in midterm races in recent months appear to violate those laws. In Tennessee, several campaigns have been hit with AI attack ads, even after the state passed a law requiring disclosure in deepfake political ads in July. Just weeks after that law passed, a dark money group opposing GOP governor candidate Marsha Blackburn aired an ad using AI without disclosure showing her cavorting with pharma lobbyists, tarring her as “Queen Mama Pharma” and tying her to opioid deaths in the state. Blackburn’s campaign sent a cease-and-desist letter to the group calling the ad false and defamatory and successfully got several TV stations to take the ad off the air. In the state’s 6th Congressional District, two competing Republican candidates also attacked each other with dueling AI-powered ads. Johnny Garrett aired an ad showing someone with the nametag of his rival, Van Hilleary, receiving a stack of money from Michael Bloomberg, while Hilleary’s campaign hit back with an ad showing Garrett sleeping in office and attending a pride parade. Both campaigns told local media that they believed the new deepfake law didn’t apply to candidates for federal office. In Michigan, meanwhile, El-Sayed’s campaign has sharply criticized the AI-made ad, which seeks to closely link the candidate to the Muslim Brotherhood and Piker, a left-wing Twitch streamer. A spokesperson for The Front Line Action, the super PAC behind the ad, defended the spot. “The substance of the ad is grounded in El-Sayed’s own public statements and documented reporting and records concerning him and individuals associated with or supportive of his campaign,” the PAC spokesperson said in a statement. Also disputed: Which statute applies to the ad. One Michigan law requires a three-second voiceover acknowledging AI’s use in political commercials and a four-second written disclosure. A second election law, governing “materially deceptive media,” however, also requires disclosure throughout a video if it “falsely represents a depicted individual,” intends to harm a candidate’s electoral chances and is distributed within 90 days of an election. Additionally, the person distributing the ad has to know that it falsely represents the person depicted. A PAC spokesperson said the group views the first law as governing its ad and said the commercial is in compliance. Efforts to prohibit the distribution of deceptive AI-generated ads or mandate disclosures of AI use in advertising have failed to gain traction in Congress or with the Federal Election Commission, which currently lacks a quorum to operate anyway. And legal experts say there are high hurdles to regulating political speech, particularly when ads reflect words that the targeted candidates actually uttered. Generally, AI-generated ads that can be interpreted as satire or parody are exempt from the state disclosure requirements, said Ilana Beller, director of state AI governance and technology at Public Citizen, the left-leaning consumer advocacy group. The organization has advocated for regulation at the federal and state level. Federal judges in Hawaii and California found parts of election deepfake laws in those states unconstitutional on First Amendment grounds. But even without federal action, the growing number of state regulations seems to have helped limit what Beller called the “nightmare scenario” of truly deceptive, realistic-looking commercials in which “the public sees a thing and believes that the candidate actively participated in something morally wrong or scandalous in some way that would sway public opinion.” A changing campaign playbook Controversies aside, AI has had the broad effect of lowering the barrier to entry to political ad-making. Political advertisers and observers said that ad-makers have been turning to AI to streamline their process, saving money and time by testing AI versions of ads that, if approved, go into real production. Lauren French, the communications director of Senate Majority PAC, a leading Democratic group, said that while some political campaigns have always used ads to promote lies, they’re now “doing it with tools that were previously not available.” She criticized the ads attacking Talarico and Ossoff as misleading voters. “We still need to embrace it and use it,” she said of the new technology. “But we can use it and be ethical, tell the truth.” Meanwhile, other campaigns airing ads featuring genuine videos of their opponents have taken the time to explicitly declare that they aren’t generated by AI — in an attempt to help viewers cut through the slop. “I’m going to show you something, no AI, no special effects, just Michael Whatley in his own words,” Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper declared at the beginning of one attack ad aired earlier this year. Persily, the Stanford professor, said voters could eventually get so used to AI attacks that they would grow to doubt even real videos. “It is going to be increasingly difficult for voters to know whether something is true or not,” he said. “That’s the greater harm to democracy.”

cnn.com.title: Trump announced a $54 billion energy investment from South Korea. South Korea said he jumped the gun
cnn.com.text: South Korea has pushed back against a $54 billion investment announced by the Trump administration, turning a struggling project to export natural gas from Alaska into another potential sticking point in the allies’ long-running negotiations over trade. On Wednesday Trump touted the figure as part of a broader agreement for Seoul to invest $200 billion in US energy in exchange for lower tariffs on South Korean goods. But South Korea later said it had given no firm commitment to the Alaska project. “Putting figures or using definitive language goes far beyond what was agreed,” Minister of Trade Industry and Resources Kim Jung-kwan said Thursday, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap. According to a statement from the US Department of Commerce on Wednesday, South Korea and the US had agreed to “commence working” on the Alaska project, “subject to commercial reasonableness.” It gave no figure for how much South Korea would invest in it. CNN has reached out to the US Department of Commerce for comment. The discrepancy between official accounts indicates clashing priorities that could hinder further negotiations between Washington and Seoul. Relations between the long-term allies have become strained since Trump returned to office, including over the arrest of nearly 500 people, mostly Korean nationals, during an ICE raid at a Hyundai plant in Georgia that sparked outrage back home. The car maker is one of South Korea’s largest companies. In the US, energy security has become a focal point ahead of November’s midterm elections, as the war in Iran has hit global oil supply and increased the cost of gas and other everyday purchases. And in Alaska, the pipeline project – estimated to cost between $45 and $55 billion – has entered the close Senate race between GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. On Wednesday, Sullivan’s office hailed what it described as the “historic $54 billion investment by South Korea” into the Alaska LNG project. CNN has called Sullivan’s office for further comment. In a break from her party’s policies, Peltola has thrown her support behind the Alaska LNG project as way to lower energy costs for Alaskans. Energy security South Korea is the world’s third-largest importer of liquefied natural gas. After the war in Iran disrupted Middle East supplies, Asian energy importers started buying more LNG from the US, which has become the world’s largest producer and exporter. Kim, the Korean minister, said the country would carefully review whether to proceed with the Alaska LNG project. A joint statement said the US would facilitate the favorable involvement of Korean vendors if the project went through, and grant priority access to its LNG supply. “The government will continue to put the national interest as priority and do its best to ensure that economic and trade relations between South Korea and the US develop into a stable and predictable partnership,” Kim added. But the capital-intensive Alaska project, which would include 807 miles of pipeline and an LNG export facility, has been under development for over a decade and delayed by a lack of financing and purchase agreements.

cnn.com.title: The US economy added just 29,000 jobs last month and the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%
cnn.com.text: The US labor market hit a soft patch in September as the economy added just 29,000 jobs and the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%, new Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed Friday. The latest jobs report – and the final official employment snapshot before the midterm elections – also showed that recent months’ hiring was weaker than previously thought and that wage growth slowed, putting Americans’ paychecks further behind the 8-ball at a time when inflation has accelerated. Through September, the economy has added an average of 68,000 jobs per month, BLS data shows. That’s stronger than last year (when fewer than 10,000 jobs were added per month); however, the current pace of hiring is running well below pre-pandemic averages. All told, it remains a “low-hire, low-fire” labor market that’s undergoing a structural shift as a result of an aging population, increased Baby Boomer retirements, a decline in immigration and the advancement of artificial intelligence. September’s job gains marked a slowdown from August, when a downwardly revised 133,000 jobs were added. (Economists had previously cautioned that August’s surprisingly strong gains likely reflected some seasonal factors that overstated hiring activity.) In addition, July turned negative, with 10,000 jobs lost (previously a 21,000-job gain). Employers were expected to add about 90,000 jobs in September with an unemployment rate holding at 4.1%. Unemployment ticked up in September in part because more people entered or re-entered the labor force. The labor force participation rate moved higher last month. The annual rate of wage growth slowed for the fourth month in a row, landing at 3% in September, which is the lowest since May 2021. The job market has mostly been holding up despite a growing list of threats to hiring, from an aging population and the rapid adoption of AI to higher oil prices, policy uncertainty and the war with Iran. Stock futures surged after the jobs report release. S&P 500 futures jumped 0.9%, and futures tied to the Nasdaq 100 surged 1.3%. Dow futures rose 530 points, or 1%. Treasury yields dropped as traders digested the weaker-than-expected data and pared back bets for a Fed rate hike later this month. The 10-year yield fell to 5.18% but is still trading near multi-year highs. Traders are now pricing in just a 15% chance of a Fed rate hike in October, down from 25% one day ago, according to CME FedWatch. This story is developing and will be updated.

cnn.com.title: How El Niño will drive up the cost of foods you love
cnn.com.text: US consumers are likely to face steeper prices for their morning latte, thanks to the near-record strong super El Niño still strengthening in the Pacific Ocean. El Niño is expected to combine with preexisting supply chain pressures around the world to increase prices on tropical products such as coffee, chocolate and palm oil. But the developing countries where those products are grown are likely to face the largest impacts, said Christopher Barrett, who teaches food and agricultural economics at Cornell University. This is because developing countries have less capacity to adapt to shortages of key agricultural products like fertilizer, poor harvests of maize and other staple crops, and less resilience to bounce back from extreme weather and climate events. 🌧️ Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app. This El Niño, which is forecast to peak this fall and winter, comes at an already challenging time for food prices, given supply chain pressures from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Black Sea. “We’re not in normal times,” Barrett said. This makes the ongoing El Niño somewhat of a food supply wild card. Still, many experts expect El Niño to cause localized food supply crises, particularly in eastern and southern Africa, while global impacts remain more limited. Trouble in the tropics El Niño is a periodic climate cycle that features hotter-than-normal sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean. The effects of El Niño reverberate around the globe, bringing drought to some regions, such as Australia, and flooding to others, including eastern Africa, along with an increased prevalence of heat extremes worldwide. Coffee and palm oil-producing countries are particularly exposed to El Niño’s impacts because of their geography. Brazil and Vietnam are major coffee-growing regions, and both can see significant shifts in precipitation during an El Niño, as can other growing areas in Central America. In fact, El Niño is already driving flooding in Southeast Asia and drought in Central America, and it’s still at least three to four months away from its forecast peak. Palm oil is mainly grown in parts of Asia and is used as an ingredient in a wide variety of foods and other products — including cosmetics and biofuels. Indonesia, a major palm oil producer, is experiencing an El Niño-related drought, as the region’s typically heavy precipitation has shifted elsewhere. Indonesia is also seeing significant wildfire outbreaks, with this fire season currently on track to rival the worst on record there, which occurred during a previous super El Niño in 2015 to 2016. These wildfires are hurting palm oil production, too. Because it’s used in so many different products, a shortage of palm oil could lead to higher prices in areas well beyond the growing regions, including the US. Food security experts do not anticipate food shortages within the US from El Niño, given the country’s ample agricultural production. But the cost of these particular food products may increase during the rest of 2026 and into 2027 and beyond. El Niño makes a bad supply chain worse Maximo Torero, chief economist at the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, said global food prices are already on a steady climb because of the combination of geopolitical tensions, trade barriers and now El Niño. The big question though is how much El Niño will further amplify food prices, with a large range of projected increases depending on its severity and on countries’ policy responses. For example, the oil supply crisis tied to the Iran conflict is increasing the costs of gasoline and diesel fuel and limiting fertilizer supplies. Meanwhile, trade barriers put in place by the US and other nations are affecting the price of goods from many countries. According to Barrett, trade can be thought of as a “release valve” when facing the effects of El Niño. Trade barriers could constrain countries’ abilities to absorb El Niño-related extreme weather events and lead to some food price increases, particularly at the national or regional level. For example, Torero said El Niño has already resulted in cuts to food production forecasts. A drier-than-average monsoon season has reduced India’s rice harvest, and Australia’s important wheat crop is also projected to come in lower than usual for the year as conditions turn drier and hotter than average there. If India decides to limit rice exports due to concerns about domestic food insecurity, that will in turn increase global rice prices. “My view right now is that we are moving slowly towards a food crisis that will be hitting us at the end of this year, beginning of next year. How deep it is will depend a lot on the additional factor of El Niño,” Torero said. That analysis, he said, assumes that the conflicts over the Strait of Hormuz and the war between Russia and Ukraine will continue. Nelson Villoria, an agricultural economist at Kansas State University, said there can be a time lag between an El Niño and its effects on food prices. “Tropical commodities such as palm oil, coconut oil, coffee and fishmeal, show the largest increases,” he said. With vegetable oils and coffee, prices can stay elevated for up to a year after an El Niño. Villoria said that globally, cereal crops tend not to be sensitive to El Niño-related effects, because much of the industrialized world doesn’t see major extreme weather impacts on those crops. However, it’s a different story in parts of Africa. “Maize in Southern and Eastern Africa are highly sensitive, and their prices may spike considerably, up to ~20%, with dire consequences for the people in those regions,” he said. Eastern Africa can be susceptible to flooding during an El Niño, drowning cereal crops there, while southern Africa is drought-prone. These areas are relatively disconnected from world markets, making it harder to simply increase food imports to cover shortages. “Food prices almost always go up a bit with El Niño events, and they go up more the more serious the El Niño and the worse the timing,” said Barrett of Cornell University. This one is likely to be the most intense El Niño on record, “crazy big,” and is hitting the global economy at a particularly bad time, he said.

cnn.com.title: Trump administration shifts funds from human rights to supporting far-right causes
cnn.com.text: The US State Department directed millions of dollars originally earmarked to promote human rights to promote far-right causes including Afrikaner rights in South Africa, safeguarding “Western civilizational norms,” and documenting “backsliding” in Europe related to mass migration, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. The funds, which come from the nearly $177 million in Democracy Funds, were obligated despite concerns and holds by the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the source said. They were due to lapse on Wednesday, the last day of the fiscal year. The proposed causes align with the Trump administration’s broader shifts away from traditional human rights to focus on causes like alleged free-speech suppression and mass migration in Europe as well as “natural rights.” Two of the proposed grants are focused on Brazil and South Africa – countries where the administration has clashed with the governments – and a third is focused on Nigeria, where the administration has alleged “mass slaughter” of Christians. It marks another instance of the administration bypassing Congress on funding matters, following its move to cancel $810 million of funding that has been appropriated by Congress for refugees, immigrants and other services. Typically, the money from the Democracy Funds is used to support programs in authoritarian countries or those with limited democracies, the source said. Instead, the proposed grants, which were first reported by The Guardian, include funding for programs in Europe and the United Kingdom. Asked about the funds, an unnamed State Department spokesperson said they had completed congressional notification requirements. “The President promised to combat the destructive woke agenda that has done so much damage to our country and to the world,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said. “We will never apologize for defending Western civilization, opposing censorship, ending the era of mass migration, and taking action against government-sponsored race-based discrimination in South Africa.” According to the source familiar with the matter, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had signed off on a memo to obligate the funds despite the ongoing holds. Senate Foreign Relations Committee ranking member Sen. Jeanne Shaheen had put holds on 10 proposed awards worth a total of $22 million. The grants have buy-in from the highest levels of the White House, including Vice President JD Vance, the source said. The White House referred to the State Department for comment. “Congress appropriated money for the Democracy Fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” Shaheen in a statement. “In bypassing Congress, the Trump Administration is now using taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies,” the New Hampshire Democrat said. “This is a waste of resources and undermines American values and our relationships with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.” The proposed grants that had holds include one to combat alleged judicial overreach and censorship in Brazil. The Trump administration has clashed with the Lula government and had imposed sanctions on Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the trial of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally. The sanctions were lifted in December. However, the US has also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US and President Donald Trump has met with Flávio Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro’s son who is running for president in Brazil. Other proposed grants focus on Europe, including a $5 million award to support the development of “a civilizational alliance in Europe through research, public debates, and policy reform to safeguard freedom of expression, political competition, and national sovereignty.” Top administration officials, including Vance, have lambasted European nations over allegations of free speech backsliding while also meeting with far-right European political figures. Samuel Samson, a top appointee in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, argued last year for the need for “civilizational allies” in Europe. “Our hope is that both Europe and the United States can recommit to our Western heritage, and that European nations will end the weaponization of government against those seeking to defend it,” he wrote. The Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor has undergone significant changes under the second Trump administration. As CNN reported last year, the US State Department will require its diplomats describe enforcement of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies, alleged facilitation of mass migration, and government funding that supports abortion medications as “human rights infringements” in its next human rights report. The report will also shift focus to “natural rights” like freedom of speech, an official said at the time, in a move likely to target traditional European allies for alleged freedom of speech restrictions.

cnn.com.title: With a steel mill and campaign cash, Trump and GOP leaders launch an Iowa rescue mission
cnn.com.text: Republicans are on a rescue mission in Iowa, touting new plans for a $15 billion steel mill as President Donald Trump and the state’s GOP leaders rush to blunt the political impact of a battered economy and prevent the governor’s office, a Senate seat and three House seats from slipping into Democratic hands in November. Gov. Kim Reynolds called the Republican-led state legislature into a special session set to begin Friday — days after Trump unveiled the proposed eastern Iowa steel mill in the Oval Office. Lawmakers are set to meet to amend the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction program to pave the way for state incentives for the plant near the Mississippi River in Lee County. Trump’s announcement came the same week the Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP’s super PAC, announced it was spending another $20 million in Iowa to boost the Senate campaign of US Rep. Ashley Hinson, who polls show is locked in a tight race against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek. The move brings GOP spending in Iowa to more than $100 million. “For me, it’s always been about going out and earning every vote and running like I’m 10 points behind, which I don’t think I am,” Hinson told CNN on Thursday. She conceded that rising costs are taking a toll, adding: “We do need to bring prices down. We need to figure out how we provide relief to working families.” The battle Republicans face in Iowa — a state Trump won by 13 percentage points just two years ago — is a window into the party’s broader challenges across the Midwest, where Trump’s war with Iran has sent gas and diesel prices soaring and his trade battles have strained manufacturers’ budgets, increased household costs and limited farmers’ access to foreign markets. Iowa-based conservative talk radio host Steve Deace sounded the alarm last week, taking to social media to warn Republicans that “that this might end being an even worse midterm environment than 2006” — the year Democrats gained six Senate seats and 31 House seats to take majorities in both chambers. Deace called the war in Iran a “political albatross.” “We are risking what’s left of the Trump presidency on this, because if Democrats take control the legislative branch the Trump domestic agenda we all voted for will largely cease,” he said. Deace urged Republicans to turn attention toward unpopular Democratic positions, while also articulating what victory in Iran would look like. “The political environment is constantly shifting,” said Johnson County GOP Chairwoman Teresa Bumgartner. “At this point, we have to be focused on the elements that we can control — which is getting our message out.” Steel plant skepticism The fallout from the steel plant announcement — and the president’s pledge to visit Iowa in the closing month of the campaign to tout the project — has injected a wild card into the final weeks of the midterm election. A promise of creating 1,750 permanent jobs, along with 6,000 temporary construction jobs, comes with a wave of suspicion from Republicans and Democrats alike. “It sounds too good to be true, and it just might be,” a top Republican official in Iowa told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to avoid agitating the Trump administration. From talk radio to editorial pages of the state’s newspapers, praise and skepticism of the project has been dominating the political conversation this week in Iowa. The announcement was met with comparisons to FoxConn, the Taiwanese electronic giant that fell far short of delivering on plans to spend $10 billion on a Wisconsin plant that would employ 13,000 — a development Trump in 2017 hailed as part of a rebirth of American manufacturing. “I’m from Wisconsin, home of ‘FoxConn.’ Good luck with your steel mill,” Jason Maloney of Washburn, Wisconsin, wrote in a letter to the editor in the Des Moines Register. “Is a steel mill really coming to landlocked Iowa? People of Iowa, prepare to be grifted.” Asked whether the project could become an Iowa version of FoxConn, Hinson told CNN: “I don’t think so. I trust our governor who has been working on this deal for months to make sure that we get secure that investment here in Iowa.” While Democrats said they were supportive of the economic development potential, they acknowledged hearing a wave of concern from skeptical Iowans about whether the project was an election-year gambit or something that would actually come to fruition. Rob Sand, the state auditor who is the Democratic candidate for governor, said he welcomed the creation of jobs, but was reserving judgment until learning more details. “I want to make sure this is a real opportunity,” Sand, who is facing GOP businessman and farmer Zach Lahn in the race to replace Reynolds, told reporters in Des Moines, “but also at the end of the day Iowa is getting served by it and not getting fleeced.” Brad Moudry, who owns a commercial electric business in northern Iowa, said he hoped Iowa lawmakers did their homework on the proposed plant, but said it “sounded good” and could have a trickle-down effect into the broader economy. “It’s going to take a lot of infrastructure.
