If they’re going to create 1,600 jobs, is there enough housing for all those people?” said Moudry, a Trump supporter who has been following news of the announcement this week. “It’s going to be a win-win no matter what, but people have to give it a little time.” The project now is squarely intertwined with the fight for control of Congress, which also runs directly through Iowa. The fiercely-competitive Senate race, along with three House seats, could play a pivotal role in whether Republicans maintain their narrow majorities in Washington. The Trump factor Just days after Hinson became the latest Republican seeking to distance herself from Trump by calling for an “immediate and successful end to the war in Iran,” she was reeled back in. Standing in the Oval Office a few feet from the president, Hinson praised the steel project, telling the president: “I appreciate your agenda.” Yet as Hinson campaigned in northeastern Iowa on Thursday, she renewed her call for an end to the Iran war “to provide immediate relief to Iowa families right now,” but she did not mention the steel project. Only when a reporter in Waterloo asked about the project did she briefly mention it, calling the plant “an amazing opportunity for our state.” Hinson now faces a delicate dance – replicated by many Republicans across the country – of trying to reap the benefits of Trump by motivating his supporters without being carried away by a political undertow of those exhausted by his second term. Turek is among the Iowa lawmakers who will vote on the proposed steel mill Friday. He said he looked forward to learning more details, saying: “We need jobs more than ever.” But he signaled his intent to keep trying to tie his opponent to policies of the Trump administration. “Gas and diesel prices have risen more here than almost any other state in the country. We are all paying the price,” Turek said in a new ad released Wednesday. “Ashley Hinson has voted over and over for policies that have jacked up prices, while she gets richer and richer.” A bleak era for Iowa Democrats For Iowa Democrats, the last election cycle worth truly celebrating came in 2018 — two years before Caitlin Clark arrived on campus in Iowa City. That year, the midterm elections of Trump’s first term, Democrats won three US House seats in Iowa — ousting incumbent Republicans in two of them — but narrowly lost the governor’s race to Reynolds. Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in Iowa since 2008, when former President Barack Obama was on the ballot, the first of two times Obama won the state in a general election. Not since 1968 has Iowa seen a wide-open race for governor and Senate at the same time, which is one of the factors driving the state’s fiercely competitive election cycle. The decision by two of the state’s top Republicans, Sen. Joni Ernst, and Reynolds, a two-term governor, not to seek third terms has created a rare opening for Democrats. Yet Democrats still face challenges of their own, including 180,000 fewer registered voters than Republicans. September voter registration data from the Iowa secretary of state shows that 711,990 voters are registered with the Republican Party, with 529,275 voters registered as Democrats and 564,581 voters not affiliated with either major political party. Independents remain the most important wild card. Early voting data is offering Iowa Democrats reason for optimism. Democrats have made 67% of ballot requests, up from 54% at this point in 2024. April Melton, the chairwoman of the Black Hawk County GOP, said she thinks Republicans will “buck history” and deliver Trump a strong midterm performance — in part, she said, because she believes the president deserves credit for decisively taking action against Iran without putting American troops on the ground there. “All we’re doing is paying a little extra in gas,” she said. But Melton said she sees the midterms much like recent Iowa-versus-Iowa State college football games: razor-tight and likely to be won in the final minutes. “Fight like you’re losing, always,” Melton said.

cnn.com.title: Suspects bought meat mincer and electric saw before socialite’s murder, court hears
cnn.com.text: Days before Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi was killed, her father-in-law and brother-in-law allegedly went on an ominous shopping spree. An electric saw, a meat mincer and a refrigerator were among the items they bought in preparation for the killing and disposal of the mother of four, prosecutors told a Hong Kong court Friday. The gruesome 2023 murder of Choi, who rubbed shoulders with showbiz elites at fashion events and had a significant online following, sent shockwaves through the wealthy financial hub and made global headlines. Only parts of Choi’s body were recovered, deepening the mystery at the time surrounding the violent death of the prominent young socialite. Her ex-husband Alex Kwong, his brother Anthony Kwong and their father Kwong Kau have pleaded not guilty to her murder during a trial that is shedding new light on Choi’s final moments. Lead prosecutor Charlotte Draycott told jurors on Friday that the model and influencer was struck repeatedly in the head with a hammer inside a car driven by her former brother-in-law, with her ex-husband also inside. She had been on her way to pick up her daughter from school. Prosectors allege planned attack About two weeks before Choi’s death, Kwong Kau and his son Anthony Kwong, who also worked as Choi’s driver, were seen visiting several shops and buying an array of items directly linked to the murder, Draycott told the court. The items included an electric saw, a meat mincer as well as some boxes and a refrigerator, along with a large chopping board, a giant saucepan and some deodorizing supplies. Parts of Choi’s body were later found inside the refrigerator, Draycott said. A hammer bought by Anthony Kwong is believed to be the murder weapon, Draycott said, while Choi’s ex-husband allegedly borrowed from a friend the vehicle where the murder is said to have taken place, according to the prosecution. “This is why we say this is a cogitated plan as each person played their part in getting the premises ready,” Draycott told the court. On February 21, 2023, Choi was due to pick up her daughter from school. Shortly before the planned school run, Anthony and Alex met at a Starbucks, where CCTV captured Anthony making a series of gestures that Draycott suggested may have foreshadowed the attack. Footage showed him appearing to hold something down with both hands before moving his right arm up and down, the prosecutor said. “You may interpret that [Anthony] was indicating to [Alex] how he could pull Abby’s head down,” she told jurors as they viewed the CCTV footage. She added that Anthony later picked Choi up, while Alex joined the vehicle at another location. During the journey, Choi exchanged text messages with her mother-in-law. The messages stopped at 2:44 pm. Draycott said Choi was then attacked with the hammer inside the vehicle. Jurors were shown the alleged weapon, along with autopsy photographs documenting Choi’s injuries. “The blows were savage,” she told the court. The white vehicle carrying Choi, according to Draycott, pulled up at a house in a rural area of Hong Kong, close to the border with mainland China. She added that Choi’s blood was found in the vehicle together with Alex and Anthony Kwong’s DNA. Kwong Kau is alleged to have arranged to have rented the property. “They were not worried. They were not upset. It’s what they expected,” the prosecutor said, as she showed footage of Kwong Kau clad in a surgical mask near the vehicle. Later that day, a neighbor reported electric saw noises and an odor, Draycott said, adding that all items purchased by the father-in-law and the brother-in-law were eventually recovered in the village house. Anthony Kwong and Kwong Kau were arrested days later while Alex was subsequently arrested at a ferry pier just before he tried to flee Hong Kong, Draycott said. The trial continues Friday afternoon and is expected to last for eight weeks.

cnn.com.title: Thailand’s soft power play: Culture as global currency
cnn.com.text: Asia’s growing soft-power, led most visibly by Japan and South Korea through cultural exports such as anime and K-pop, has helped drive global interest in the region and intensified competition for tourists within it. In Southeast Asia, Thailand has long been the destination of choice for many travelers, but by investing in infrastructure, introducing flexible visa policies, and expanding aviation access, neighboring countries have gained ground.  Malaysia in June overtook Thailand as the regions’ most visited nation.  To regain momentum, the Thai government and its citizens are reintroducing the country to the world and diving into their soft power strengths. Thailand’s “T-wave,” a term used to describe the country’s soft power influence has recently grown. Once primarily defined by Thai food, in 2023, under former Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin, the National Soft Power Strategy Committee (NSPSC) was created to focus on 13 key areas including food, festivals, music, film, fashion, and tourism. In the years since, the Thai government has supported initiatives in the film industry, providing cash rebates for production crews’ local spending and hiring. These policies have attracted multimillion-dollar projects such as season three of HBO’s “The White Lotus” and Universal Pictures’ “Jurassic World: Rebirth,” whose productions used the country’s tropical backdrops. HBO, like CNN, is owned by Warner Bros. Discovery. The effect was immediate and impactful. Filmed on Koh Samui, “The White Lotus” drove an 88% jump in online searches and a 300% tourism increase to the island. “We’ve seen a very strong upsurge in entertainment media that has really continued to drive the narrative of Thailand tourism,” says Steve Johnson, an executive at the Tourism Authority of Thailand’s branch in New York. When speaking about Thai entertainment, Lalisa Manobal is often mentioned. The music megastar known globally as LISA, made her acting debut in season three of “The White Lotus” but already had an international following as a member of the girl group BLACKPINK. Her solo release “SaWaDiKa,” titled after a Thai female greeting, amassed over 100 million views on YouTube within two days of its release in September. “If I ask almost anybody on the planet, ‘What is Thailand?’ They will probably mention Lalisa,” says Dr. Daniele Carminati, a lecturer at Mahidol University International College (MUIC) in Salaya township, who specializes in soft power and public diplomacy. Similar to BTS in Korea, he says LISA shows how cultural figures can carry a country’s image across borders. Featuring Muay Thai martial arts fighters, tuk-tuks, and traditional Thai dress, the “SaWaDiKa” music video makes familiar cultural symbols accessible to millions through a global pop package. Where Thailand and its culture are becoming increasingly accessible to new audiences through global and domestic dramas, films, and music, experienced travelers in Thailand are often drawn to its wellness options.  The country’s tourism board sees it as a competitive advantage within the region. “We are the mecca in Southeast Asia as it pertains to wellness,” says Johnson, alluding to Thailand’s place as the seventh-fastest growing wellness market in the $6.8 trillion wellness economy. From hot springs, to detox retreats and herbalist practices, wellness in Thailand extends far beyond massages or yoga at luxury resorts. From Chiang Mai to Hua Hin, “Everywhere [in Thailand] has a unique wellness feature that they promote,” says Johnson. In a 2025 speech, the current Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra said, “we are positioning Thailand as a global wellness hub, offering not just treatment but an experience of better well-being.” The question is, whether cultural appeal can translate into longer-term economic benefits. Although the T-wave is closely modeled after the K-wave in South Korea, it remains to be seen whether Thailand can emulate Korea’s economic success. Speaking about the country’s prospects, William J. Jones, an assistant professor of international relations at MUIC, says, “Thailand has incredible potential. Its historical strength is being an open society, an open economy, welcoming to people,” which can attract tourists and businesses alike. But he cautions that tourism-led growth can be fragile, and going beyond it requires broader economic development, government investment and policy execution. Thailand wants to be “a digital hub, an AI hub, an aviation hub,” says Jones, but so do many of its neighbors.  The difference, he suggests, will come down to implementation. For all of Thailand’s technology and tourism ambitions, its more distinctive advantage may be one that is more difficult to engineer: the culture that  travelers encounter on the ground. Turning that appeal into a lasting economic influence may depend on whether Thailand can build on what already draws people to it. Thailand’s enduring power, says Jones, is still “its culture, its food, its landscape.”

cnn.com.title: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
cnn.com.text: Smit Machchhar, the hero Flydubai captain who fought off a savage attack by his copilot, kept fighting because he could not “let everybody else die,” he said in his first public remarks since Wednesday’s suspected hijacking attempt. “In that moment, I was fighting for my life,” Machchhar told India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was so severely wounded that I had fallen down… at that time, I was thinking what if I don’t get up?” A horrific mid-air catastrophe on flight FZ 1073 heading to Tel Aviv was averted in a stunning turn of events on Wednesday when passengers bravely rushed into the cockpit and stand-in pilots regained control of the aircraft. Machchhar was badly injured while trying to fend off the attacker. Images showed a gruesome scene onboard, with blood splashed across the cockpit and the seriously wounded pilot lying on the floor, his pained face partially covered with a mask. Machchhar told Modi he was on the ground in the cockpit when he realized the plane was going down. “And I knew in that moment – one last push, Smit! Just do it. The door is right there,” he said. “And even at that time, he was beating me up.” “And then I just opened it… and then everybody came,” he said, referring to several other passengers who then rushed into the cockpit and restrained his attacker. “I was doing this for my life, but at the same time, I knew that I couldn’t let everybody else die.” Modi praised Machchhar’s heroics, telling the veteran pilot that his “courage, patience and quick thinking… saved the lives of so many people.” “You yourself were fighting the battle of life and death,” Modi said. Machchhar is recovering at a hospital in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). He was initially treated for his injuries in Saudi Arabia, where the diverted plane was forced to make an emergency landing. The father of two had suffered “massive blood loss” and was “severely wounded,” dentist Shota Musaev, a passenger on the flight who helped treat him, previously told CNN. His bravery “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN on Wednesday. Machchhar appeared emotional in the call with Modi while recalling the ordeal, and apologized to the prime minister for crying on the phone. The two later spoke in Gujarati, the language predominantly spoken by people from India’s western state of Gujarat, which is where Modi is from. Machchhar said his daughter had come to visit him in hospital but got scared seeing him in his condition. His youngest son, who is two, has not been able to meet him yet, he said. Born into a family in the textile business, becoming a pilot wasn’t Machchhar’s “childhood dream,” he told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast in 2025. Initially, he’d enrolled in a textile engineering course after school. Speaking to Modi, Machchhar said he felt a sense of pride. “Now that you have called me, I am really really proud of myself,” Machchhar said. “I wasn’t proud before this, but now I am.” His wife, Sonal Machchhar, told CNN affiliate CNN News18 that the family had not asked him yet about what happened because “we don’t want him to get flashbacks of the incident.” “We want him to fully recover, and I’m sure once he is in the right space to talk, he will share it with everyone of how the incident went on with him,” Sonal Machchhar said. What we know about the suspect The plane’s co-pilot and Machchhar’s alleged attacker has now been transferred from Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed, to the UAE, where he faces a terrorism investigation. A top UAE official on Friday described the mid-flight crisis as a “dangerous terrorist act.” Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic adviser to the UAE’s president, also cautioned against conspiracy theories as investigators look to establish the facts surrounding what happened. The suspect is an Omani national, Netanyahu told CNN Thursday. Oman and Israel do not have formal diplomatic relations, and it is not yet clear how the Omani pilot would have obtained clearance to fly to Israel. Authorities are yet to divulge the co-pilot’s identity. And there hasn’t been any confirmation of his motive or of the weapon he used in the violent altercation, though Netanyahu suggested to Fox News this might have been a knife or an axe. In a video posted on his social media platforms Friday, Netanyahu said the alleged attacker had “undergone Islamist radicalization.” “He intended to crash the plane with its passengers on board,” he said. “We are investigating whether he was sent by someone, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price,” Netanyahu continued. In comments to Fox News on Thursday, the Israeli leader said that it was too soon to say whether the attacker had connections to Iran or anyone else, although this would be established one way or another in the coming days. So far, he has stopped short of describing the incident as a terrorist act. Netanyahu said the attacker was suicidal, adding that he had called out “kill me” after being restrained by other passengers. US President Donald Trump suggested later Thursday the pilot may be linked to Iran, though he provided no details. This story had been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: With a new breed of candidate, Democrats are challenging in states they usually lose
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump’s flagging popularity isn’t the only problem Republicans face this fall. A slate of strong Democratic hopefuls is putting in play Senate races long assumed to be heading for the Republican column. Stumbling GOP candidates in several pivotal contests, meanwhile, threaten to turn a tough November into an electoral collapse. After years of struggling to connect with voters, some Democratic recruits have expanded the battlefield and are beginning to redress the failures in positioning, policy and language that helped fuel Trump’s dominance. This is giving the party resurgent hopes of the net gain of four seats it needs to control the Senate, even as it moves into prime position to win a House majority next month. In North Carolina, polls show two-term former Gov. Roy Cooper is popular with independents and is sufficiently competitive in rural areas to dent GOP margins. In a more surprising turn, Iowa state legislator Josh Turek, a self-declared “common sense prairie populist,” is making a race of it in a state where the president romped home by 13 points only two years ago. In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, another candidate representing generational change, has created a distinct political persona with disdainful critiques of Trump. His swing-state success and rising national profile have stirred speculation he may be what his party is looking for in the 2028 presidential campaign. In Texas, James Talarico is testing out a bespoke infusion of economic populism and Christian faith to conjure Democratic hopes that the ever-shimmering mirage of a statewide victory can become reality for the first time in 30 years. In Ohio, which Trump won at a canter in 2024, former Sen. Sherrod Brown has found that his perennial message of blue-collar populism is meeting its moment as an increasingly distant president pals around with billionaires. Each of these candidates, is, in their own ways, seeking to capture something beyond Trump’s unpopularity and a sense of national economic unease; they are also trying to reinvent the brand of a party that squandered voter trust in recent years and drove some of its core voters toward the Republican president. A roster of strong candidates is especially important to Democrats this year because the country still views the party largely negatively. A CNN/SSRS survey in late July showed that the public favors Democrats this fall by 8 points, but congressional Democrats and Republicans are about equally unpopular and there are low hopes for what possible Democratic majorities might achieve. Some GOP candidate choices aren’t helping Some Democrats lucked out with problematic GOP opponents — like MAGA champion Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia and scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton in Texas, who were backed by Trump over the reservations of establishment GOP leaders. In North Carolina, Michael Whatley is well known within GOP circles as a former Republican National Committee chair, but he has toiled to match Cooper’s name recognition. Sometimes circumstances threaten to overwhelm even candidates regarded as well suited to their races. In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a relatable former TV anchor and strong communicator, is immersed in the state’s key issues. She’d normally be a favorite to win the Senate seat soon to be vacated by Joni Ernst, but the farm state is being hammered by Trump’s tariffs and high fuel costs. Of course, any candidate can look like a genius if they win. And losers are always second-guessed. The most intriguing Senate race may be in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed is the most high-risk Democratic candidate in a critical race. If he wins, the 41-year-old epidemiologist will be a herald of a new political generation and star of the progressive movement. But if former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers prevails, left-wing Democratic base voters who rejected the more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens will be accused of throwing away a seat, and possibly the Senate. Candidates who blend skill, discipline and relatability while crossing ideological lines are like gold dust. But there are two even more important qualities: luck and timing. Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has often seemed to possess mythical survival qualities. But she’s facing her toughest reelection race yet in a dark national environment for Republicans. The clamor of the Trump era has roughed up her reputation for independence and forced choices that drag her between her base and more moderate voters — like her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Now she’s being branded by her Democratic opponent as an enabler of Trump rather than a bulwark against him. Democrats should not take their position for granted Nothing is settled a month from Election Day. Recent Senate polls show no clear leader in Texas; a slightly better picture for Democrats in Iowa; and campaigns mostly leaning toward the party in Georgia, North Carolina and Ohio. But races often narrow late. In 2024, for instance, Brown led in the Buckeye state in late September but ended up losing his Senate seat to Bernie Moreno. And who can forget the Des Moines Register/Mediacom Iowa Poll that showed Vice President Kamala Harris beating Trump a few days before he trounced her in that state by the only measure that actually matters? But Democrats are confident because the biggest influence on a midterm election remains the fortunes of the incumbent president. Trump’s low approval numbers and Americans’ concerns about high living costs, AI and the Iran war make this an especially dicey year for GOP candidates. “When the president’s party controls Congress, the president is the referendum, but the party and their candidates are the targets,” said Michael Bitzer, a professor of politics and history at Catawba College in North Carolina. Yet it’s not unusual for parties to fumble while in a good position. Trump’s backing for error-prone candidates like Mehmet Oz in Pennsylvania and Herschel Walker in Georgia in 2022, for example, helped Democrats cling onto the Senate despite then-President Joe Biden’s unpopularity. This is one reason why some in the party worry about the prospects of El-Sayed and the late replacement nominee Troy Jackson in Maine. This is also a worry in the House. Some Democrats fear that primary victories by ultra-progressive candidates may have produced nominees too radical for the electorate as the GOP warns that “communists” and “socialists” are running rampant. Most of these wins were in deeply blue states. But in California’s 22nd District, a key battleground that Trump narrowly won in 2024, Democrat Randy Villegas defeated a moderate primary rival preferred by the party’s Washington leaders. And in Maine, another progressive, Matt Dunlap, also defeated an establishment rival for the right to run in a key general election swing district. What key wins could teach Democrats for 2028 Victories by Cooper or Turek in November could give Democrats important clues about how they widen their appeal after a period up to 2024 in which their policies on immigration, gender identity issues and inflation drove away some moderate voters. Often, in the 21st century, the party’s cultural messaging appealed to the liberal cities and college-educated voters in the suburbs but alienated rural and working-class voters who once turned naturally to Democrats but deserted the party for Trump. Cooper may be their answer in one Southern state. The former governor is not running an overtly partisan Democratic campaign. He presents his candidacy as a chance for North Carolina to send an “independent” voice to the Senate. He’s using the key issue of the election — affordability — as a bridge to voters of both parties with his “Make Stuff Cost Less” tours and slogans like, “There is too much month at the end of the money.” Cooper’s earned the trust of moderates over long years in public office. He comes across as steady and understated and remembers working with Republicans in the state legislature as he courts voters who’ve tired of Trump’s chaos. It seems to be working, with polls suggesting he holds a comfortable lead over Whatley. Bitzer, who has conducted polling that confirms findings in other surveys that Cooper leads among independents, says the former governor also does far better in rural areas where the GOP typically pads out wins in a state that hasn’t voted for a Democratic presidential candidate since Barack Obama in 2008. This kind of coalition is important because polls show that while voters are looking to punish Trump, they are still skeptical of Democrats. This is one reason why elections expert Charlie Cook argues the midterms are seeing not a blue wave but a “red undertow.” Bitzer said that Cooper’s experience equips him to “recognize that (in) North Carolina … that moderate middle can tip one way or the other. And he knows how to appeal both to his party’s base, but also to that moderate middle that may split their tickets.” Turek is trying something similar in Iowa. He’s evoking the legacy of moderate Democratic Iowa Sen. Tom Harkin, who served 40 years in Congress for a state that went twice for Barack Obama and three times for Trump. He’s stressing the punishing affordability crisis, poor access to healthcare, high rates of cancer in the state and what he calls Washington “corruption.” But Turek largely avoids cultural and social issues at the center of much national Democratic and progressive messaging. He supports the Second Amendment and a strong border policy. “The Democratic brand is certainly damaged,” Turek said on a recent edition of “The Weekly Show” with Jon Stewart, describing his ideological positioning as a member of Iowa’s state legislature. “There are times where I have more agreement with my moderate Republicans on issues than with my most extreme left-wing Democrats,” he said. That stance may help shield Turek against GOP claims that the Democratic Party is careening toward its far-left flank. And if the message is a winner this fall, it may provide the party with a blueprint that stretches beyond the midterms.

cnn.com.title: At Washington’s tomb, a British royal honors the man who kicked out the Crown
cnn.com.text: On an autumn day in 1860, a bearded British man visited George Washington’s tomb at his final resting place in Virginia. While there he paused to plant a small buckeye tree. The tree would grow, and so would he, to become King Edward VII of England, King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, Emperor of India. During that humble pilgrimage, the then Prince Albert Edward, began a long tradition of members of the British royal family visiting George Washington’s Mount Vernon, a sort of reverent homage to the man who helped end British rule, and set a rot in the Empire. Over 160 years later, on a particularly warm October day the modern Prince Edward followed his Great Great Grandfather’s tradition by laying a wreath at the tomb of Washington at his Mount Vernon home. History was repeating, ancient bonds once damaged in war, silenced, and soothed in the quiet moments after. A group of tourists at Mount Vernon told the duke and the cluster of those associated with with Mount Vernon, that they had come from all over North America to share the moment, and themselves remake bonds broken some two and half centuries ago. The duke is the second senior royal to go on a pilgrimage to America this year as it celebrates its 250th birthday. In part it is a reaffirmation of America’s independence by a family who felt its less-than-harmonious divorce from British rule more than any other, and a celebration of the bonds that now exist. When King Charles III made his first visit as monarch to Washington DC earlier this year, he and US President Donald Trump highlighted the importance of the enduring “special relationship” between the US and the UK. “Ours is a partnership born out of dispute, but no less strong for it, so perhaps, in this example, we can discern that our nations are in fact instinctively like-minded – a product of the common democratic, legal and social traditions in which our governance is rooted to this day,” the king said his speech to Congress this year. During the duke’s visit to Virginia that “special relationship” returned to center stage. This week as a UK airbase used by the US military appeared under serious threat, Trump sang his special partner’s praises in partnering to hunt down the assumed attackers, saying the US was “working with Britain, it was an amazing job.” However, Trump’s announcement last week that he might ban diesel exports, including to the UK — which imports one third of its diesel from the US — became a bit of a buzz kill on the base cooperation vibe. Diesel prices on UK forecourts are the highest they’ve ever been, economists are raising the alarm and the oh-so-elusive special bond is yo-yoing toward breaking point. Christian Turner, the United Kingdom’s Ambassador to the US, who accompanied the duke as he walked in his long-dead relative’s footsteps, told CNN that these types of government issues do not affect royal visits. “As his Majesty the King said in his address to Congress it’s really a moment to step up and back and remind us that the relationship is bigger than an ambassador, a president, a duke, a secretary of state, and it’s those ties and those connections that stretch back in history and stretch forward,” the ambassador said. “It’s true, constitutionally, for us the monarchy is above politics so we’re not discussing day to day policy on trips like this, we’re thinking about those deeper ties and why still, after 250 years, we’re family.” As the prince and escorts paused to enjoy a farewell stop at the Mount Vernon Whiskey tasting, there was another subtle reminder that no matter how special the bond, even shared histories lead to different places. In this case, the spelling of the word, “Whiskey,” which in the UK is spelt with an “e” if it comes from Ireland and no “e” if it comes from Scotland. “Technically it’s either Scottish or Irish, so you’re going to have to try and work out whether you’re going to have to spell it differently to indicate it’s over here,” the duke mused. “You could replace the ‘I’ with a ‘u’,” he quipped.

cnn.com.title: Trump jokingly calls Paxton a "pain in the ass" at Texas event
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump jokingly described Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton as “a pain in the ass” during remarks in Denton, Texas, on Thursday – the latest in a long line of jabs he has made about his staunch ally who is running in a critical race for the GOP. Trump praised Paxton’s loyalty, saying that when he had faced criticism in the past, Paxton was “at my side more than anybody.” Then he quipped, “And I have to always remember that because he could be a pain in the ass sometimes. I’ll be honest.” Trump has repeatedly insulted Paxton in public remarks, even though he endorsed Paxton over a safer candidate in the Republican primary and has generally sought to boost his campaign. He has poked fun at the way the Texas attorney general dresses and talks, including at the GOP’s midterm convention, which was held in Paxton’s home state and focused heavily on him and his race. “Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said, adding: “I don’t.” Paxton has not in any way bit back – and Trump’s insults are often accompanied by praise for how Paxton does his job. But The New York Times on Wednesday published audio of Paxton privately complaining to conservative donors and lobbyists that the convention did more harm than good. “So, to be honest with you, the numbers – when we did that convention – it dropped our numbers,” the Texas attorney general said. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.” Pressed earlier Thursday by CNN’s Kristen Holmes on if he had spoken to Paxton following that leaked audio, Trump said, “No, I haven’t.” When reporters asked about the audio Wednesday afternoon during an Oval Office event, he said he hadn’t heard it. “Is he here?” Trump said in Denton. “By the way – oh, there he is. Good. I didn’t even know if he’s here.” At a later rally in Oklahoma, Trump played a clip of one of his supporters being asked about the leaked audio clip and whether Republicans are “still on board” with the president. The person in the clip responded, “100%… Get on the Trump train.” This story was updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Putin warns Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons,’ including nuclear, to protect Kaliningrad
cnn.com.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned the West against escalating the war in Ukraine, saying Moscow is prepared to use “all weapons” in its arsenal — including nuclear — if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under attack. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian leader said he had no plans to attack any European country but was prepared to respond to Western aggression if necessary and referenced the Russian territory sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. His warning follows recent military drills by NATO near Kaliningrad that the bloc has described as defensive exercises to strengthen deterrence. Those exercises have prompted strong concerns from Moscow, which warned in late September it would retaliate if NATO attempted to blockade the exclave by air or sea. “The drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another … Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,” Putin said. “If it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our country’s arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,” he cautioned. NATO, several European countries and the United Kingdom have accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare against them, including cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage attempts, aimed at breaking their support for Ukraine. Russia’s war in Ukraine, dubbed by Moscow as a “special military operation,” is now in its fifth year, but Putin shows no sign of slowing his offensive and has instead intensified strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and its capital city of Kyiv ahead of an anticipated bitterly cold winter. But recent Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s oil refineries have led to widespread fuel shortages, shattering the illusion that the consequences of the conflict are far removed from ordinary Russians. Long queues of cars at fuel stations have been seen in major cities, while hits on Russia’s largest online retailers have increased pressure on the already strained wartime economy. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky regularly refers to Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russian territory as “long-range sanctions,” designed to reduce Russia’s revenues, military capacity and push the Kremlin into negotiations. In his speech Thursday to foreign policy and international affairs academics, Putin admitted the Ukrainian strikes were taking a toll on Russia’s economy, saying they had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP) and that Ukrainian military maneuvers in the Black Sea have taken out over 100 Russian ships. However, Putin also made clear he remains undeterred. “In the Black Sea — that’s a combat zone; we struck military vessels and ships transporting military cargo, and we hardly ever made a mistake. Throughout this whole saga, they [Ukraine] have knocked out over 100 of our ships. Well, we started hitting back, and now we’re being bombarded from every direction with appeals: “Oh, please stop doing that,” Putin said. “It’s the same story with our oil refineries; they (Ukraine) openly declared their goal was to damage our economy. Did they succeed? Partially — by our estimates, we lost about one percent of our GDP. And it was done deliberately — these are civilian targets, after all. Well, they got a mirror-image response,” Putin added, sidestepping that it was Moscow who launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Putin’s admission of the economic toll comes just one day after he told newly elected members of the State Duma — the lower house of Russia’s parliament, which predictably saw the United Russia party that backs Putin hold onto its majority — that the Russian economy was stable. Taking the opportunity to swipe at Ukraine, the Russian president on Wednesday derided Kyiv’s reliance on financial assistance from its Western allies. “Mistakes, especially now, are absolutely unacceptable,” he warned parliamentarians. “Unlike some, and we won’t point fingers, Russia can’t run around the world humiliating (itself) by begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,” he said. “Firstly, because, as I have already said, it is humiliating. Secondly, no one is going to give us anything, and we know that very well. And thirdly, and most importantly, we do not need it. Russia’s financial system and economy are secure,” he continued. While signaling in recent weeks that he does not intend to draw back from the war in Ukraine, Putin also said he would prefer the conflict to end through talks. Ahead of the election, Putin had said the results would show Russians are united by the military and its goals — though the Levada Center, an independent pollster, found in an August poll that 59% of Russians favored moving to peace talks. In a further sign that Putin does not plan to slow down the “special military operation,” budget documents reviewed by Reuters show that Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.112 billion) on defense in 2027, about 27% more than originally budgeted and the highest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

cnn.com.title: Massachusetts man charged with cyberstalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller
cnn.com.text: The Justice Department charged a military veteran Thursday for allegedly making dozens of disturbing texts and calls to Katie Miller, a conservative podcaster married to White House senior adviser Stephen Miller, and her family. The man, 41-year-old John Anthony Proia III of Massachusetts, has been charged with one count of cyberstalking. He will make his initial appearance in court Thursday. Prosecutors allege that Proia used a series of phone calls to reach a “prominent member of the Republican Party” more than 40 times in a two-month period. A source familiar with the case identified the victim as Katie Miller. Proia allegedly contacted Katie Miller at all hours, sending messages that were at times graphic and threatening. He also allegedly contacted her parents, saying in one message: “My God, how can you be proud of this filth?” In another, Proia allegedly said: “Hey (first name of Victim 1’s father), how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and (first name of Victim 1’s mother). Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?” The charges followed an investigation that faced resistance within the Federal Bureau of Investigation, CNN reported. An FBI counterterrorism team in Washington initially determined that the matter did not warrant an further investigation, sources said. The investigation continued, however, and two senior agents were removed from their positions. Investigators in Boston had also expressed reservations about pursuing the case. Court documents accuse Proia of encouraging others online to place similar calls to government officials. In one post cited by prosecutors, he wrote that a online directory account “allows great latitude in finding phone numbers and addresses so you can wake folks up late at night and tell them how you feel.” “For lawful purposes, this is educational,” he added, according to the documents. In another post, Proia allegedly wrote that the wife of an unnamed cabinet official “really doesn’t like it when you prank call and tell her that he does a lot of cocaine.” In a post on X after the charge was announced, Katie Miller thanked Attorney General Todd Blanche, Massachusetts US Attorney Leah Foley, and the FBI’s Washington Field Office. CNN has reached out to Proia’s attorney for comment.

cnn.com.title: Judge blocks Trump from firing Seattle US attorney who had job for an hour
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump cannot fire US attorneys who have been appointed by courts, a federal judge in Washington state said Thursday in a first-of-its-kind ruling that tests the scope of a president’s removal power under the Constitution. The ruling comes from a lawsuit by Roger Rogoff, who was appointed by a federal court to be Seattle’s US attorney in July, only to be fired minutes later. “Mr. Roger Rogoff is the United States Attorney for the Western District of Washington and has been the rightful holder of that office since July 15, 2026, when he took the oath of office,” Judge Stanley Bastian, the chief judge of the eastern district court in Washington, said following an hourlong hearing. Courts across the country have wrestled with the administration’s efforts to keep in place so-called “interim” US attorneys selected by the president beyond the 120 days federal law allows those prosecutors to serve in the temporary role. Once that time period expires, the law gives the local federal court the power to appoint someone to serve as US attorney until the Senate confirms the president’s appointee. However, in several instances, Trump then fired that court-appointed prosecutor. Bastian said that a president’s powers to remove US attorneys under the law were limited to Senate-confirmed US attorneys – not those appointed by courts. “Allowing the president to fire a United States attorney appointed by the court also eliminates the incentive to nominate a candidate that can be confirmed by the Senate,” Bastian said. “In other words, the executive and legislative branches are supposed to and encouraged to work together.” The Justice Department does not contest a court’s ability to appoint a US attorney in that circumstance. But it argues that the president still retains the ability to fire that person. DOJ said it will appeal Bastian’s ruling. Rogoff was the first court-appointed US attorney to challenge his firing in court and Bastian noted he was the first judge ever to address the legal question of whether a president can fire court-appointed US attorneys. While Bastian’s preliminary injunction ruling is in effect, the administration cannot take steps to fire Rogoff, nor can it hinder Rogoff’s ability to carry out his duties as Seattle top federal prosecutor. Rogoff’s case ushers in a new significant legal question after months of litigation in other states over Trump’s maneuverings around US attorneys. In New Jersey for instance, Trump tried to reinstate his original choice for interim US attorney — his former criminal lawyer Alina Habba — after the federal court there selected someone else for the role. Habba later resigned after a federal appeals court said her appointment was unlawful. The Justice Department then worked with the federal judges in the state to find a prosecutor that the court could appoint to the job. Meanwhile, the Justice Department has appealed to the Supreme Court a case concerning its workarounds to keep Trump’s chosen lawyer, Sigal Chattah, as the leader of the US attorney’s office in Nevada, after lower courts said her appointment was illegal. The Supreme Court has not yet said if it will take up the Chattah case. CNN’s Kara Scannell contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Iranian accused of involvement in $3 billion hacking scheme extradited to US
cnn.com.text: An Iranian man accused of being part of a hacking scheme that breached more than 150 US universities and companies while targeting data worth over $3 billion has been extradited from Montenegro to the US to face criminal charges, police in the European country and a person familiar with the case said Thursday. Amir Barati, 40, is expected to face wire and computer fraud charges in the US Southern District of New York, where he and 16 other Iranian nationals were charged in a superseding indictment in August. Montenegrin police arrested Barati, who is also a Turkish citizen, in June at the request of the FBI. Barati’s extradition is welcome news for US law enforcement as it tries to blunt Iran’s cyber capabilities during the US’ ongoing war with the country Accused Iranian hackers rarely see a US courtroom. Barati and his co-defendants are accused of participating in a yearslong campaign that began in 2013 to steal data from universities and companies around the world, breaching about 8,000 email accounts belonging to professors in the US, Europe and elsewhere. The academic data and intellectual property the hackers targeted cost the US universities about $3.4 billion to “procure and access,” according to the indictment. CNN was unable to reach a lawyer for Barati. One of the companies allegedly victimized included the network HBO, a subsidiary of CNN’s parent company Warner Brothers Discovery. Barati allegedly helped track the progress of the hacks of universities and helped create “targeting lists” for the private sector, according to US court documents. Among the breached private US companies were 11 tech firms and two defense contractors, according to the Justice Department. Other members of the conspiracy aside from Barati allegedly hacked the Department of Labor, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the United Nations. Many of the intrusions were conducted on behalf of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, according to prosecutors. A spokesperson for the US Southern District of New York declined to comment on Thursday about Barati’s extradition. Iran’s sizable hacking capabilities have offered Tehran a way to threaten US critical infrastructure during seven months of war with the US and Israel. Over that time, Iran has been a key suspect in cyberattacks on US water systems, tank readers at gas stations, a major medical device maker and FBI Director Kash Patel’s private email account. CNN’s Kara Scannell contributed reporting.

cnn.com.title: Trump is sending $500 refund checks to nearly a million Americans. Here’s who gets them
cnn.com.text: The Affordable Care Act $500 refund checks are in the mail to nearly a million Americans, along with a letter from President Donald Trump touting his healthcare accomplishments and casting blame on his predecessor. The Treasury Department began sending the one-time payments on Wednesday to more than 950,000 Obamacare enrollees in 30 states that use the federal exchange, healthcare.gov. They will be funded through unspent user fees paid by insurers. Trump has said that these Obamacare policyholders were “wrongly overcharged” during the Biden administration – a claim that some experts dispute. The rebates are arriving a little more than a month before the midterm elections, and Republicans are fighting to maintain their control of Congress. Healthcare costs are a main concern of voters, especially as premiums and out-of-pocket costs rise for many folks. In his letter, Trump wrote, “For years, the Biden Administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov. That money belongs to hard-working Americans, not the Government, and now, I am returning it to you!” “You have paid into this flawed System, and now you are finally getting something back,” he wrote, listing his efforts to root out fraud, reduce drug prices and boost spending on rural healthcare. The refunds are going to policyholders who did not receive federal premium subsidies to buy Affordable Care Act coverage. (The vast majority of Obamacare enrollees are subsidized.) Most of the recipients are middle-class Americans who earn too much to receive subsidies this year – more than $62,600 as an individual or $128,600 for a family of four, according to the White House. Trump announced he would provide the rebates last month, the day after he promised to send $5,000 dividend payments to all Americans adults if the Republicans retain control of Congress in November’s midterm elections. It remains a question as to whether he can fulfill that promise. The move comes at a time when many Obamacare enrollees are struggling to maintain their coverage – or have dropped their policies – after congressional Republicans allowed the enhanced ACA premium subsidies to expire at the end of last year. That sent premium payments skyrocketing for many enrollees, particularly middle-income folks, for 2026. Premiums are set to jump again for 2027. Policyholders will learn how much more they’ll have to pay when open enrollment starts on November 1, just before the midterms. In a video announcing the refunds, where Trump also urged Congress to pass his healthcare plan, the president said that the $500 rebate will cover the spike in premiums “in many cases.” But some enrollees saw their monthly costs increase by far more than that, according to KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group. Unspent fees The rebates will be funded from fees that participating Obamacare insurers pay to support the federal ACA exchanges’ operations, according to the White House. The fees, which insurers pass along to enrollees in the form of higher premiums, also pay for marketing, outreach and enrollment assistance. About $1.2 billion in unspent fees had accumulated when former President Joe Biden took office in early 2021, according to an analysis by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group. The money had been adding up largely because the first Trump administration greatly reduced spending on enrollment assistance, marketing, the healthcare.gov website and the federal ACA call center. The Biden administration subsequently announced it would pour about $500 billion into these ACA operations. Enrollment roughly doubled during his term to nearly 22 million people, thanks in large part to the enhanced subsidies, which Biden signed into in early 2021. The current Trump administration is reducing the fees, which it argues will help lower premiums.

cnn.com.title: 8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president
cnn.com.text: We don’t yet know how the 2026 midterm elections will shake out. What we can say right now is that President Donald Trump’s handling of inflation is a historic liability — the likes of which we’ve rarely seen in modern American politics. As many as 8 in 10 Americans now disapprove of Trump on that issue. That’s more than disapproved of presidents for wars gone wrong, botched crisis responses and even major scandals like Watergate. A new AP-NORC poll on Thursday was the latest ugly data point for Trump. It showed Americans disapproved of him on cost-of-living issues by a stunning margin: 82% to 17%. It’s rare to get even 70% of Americans to agree on anything political. But Trump has managed to unite 8 in 10 Americans against his handling of one of the country’s most important issues. And this poll isn’t just some outlier. Here’s a brief recap of recent polls on this issue: The level of disapproval on such a major issue has few precedents, though George W. Bush did face a 77% disapproval rating in a CBS News/New York Times poll for his handling of the economy near the end of his term after the 2008 financial crisis. In 1980, the same pollster showed Jimmy Carter’s disapproval on that issue peaking at 74% amid high unemployment and inflation. One of the likeliest culprits for such high disapproval numbers would seem to be war. And those have been very unpopular. But not as unpopular as Trump’s handling of the cost of living. George W. Bush’s disapproval rating on the Iraq war peaked around 70%. Disapproval of Joe Biden’s withdrawal from Afghanistan peaked around two-thirds. And the Vietnam war led Lyndon Johnson to scrap his reelection bid in 1968, but his disapproval rating on the issue was only in the 60s. In fact, the highest disapproval rating for a war appears to be Trump’s latest numbers on the Iran war. The CNN poll showed 73% disapproved of his handling of that. When it comes to crises, as many as 64% disapproved of Bush’s handling of Hurricane Katrina, and Carter’s disapproval amid the Iran hostage crisis climbed into the mid-50s. Even Trump’s handling of the January 6 attack on the Capitol (67% in CNN polling) wasn’t as lopsided as Trump and inflation right now. As far as scandals, Ronald Reagan’s disapproval on the Iran-Contra affair reached as high as 69% in a January 1987 Washington Post-ABC News poll. And at the height of Watergate, as many as 71% of Americans disapproved of Richard Nixon on domestic issues. (We don’t have good approval polling from back then on Watergate, specifically.) Speaking of Nixon, pardons have also tested Americans’ tolerance. But even Gerald Ford’s pardon of Nixon — which was supposed to have crippled Ford politically — only saw a disapproval rating in the 50s, according to polls compiled by the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research. Indeed, about the closest Trump got previously to 80% disapproval on a major issue was another controversial set of pardons: his pardons of violent January 6 defendants last year. A Pew Research Center poll showed 74% of Americans disapproved of that. You might be noticing a trend here. Many of the issues with the highest presidential disapproval ratings involve the same president: Trump. That includes the Iran war, the January 6 Capitol attack and the related pardons. But the disapproval he faces on inflation surpasses all of those issues. You could perhaps understand why Republicans are suddenly anxious to pass legislation on affordability before the election. Trump in a new Time magazine interview published Thursday said Americans shouldn’t hold him responsible for their affordability problems and again blamed inflation on Biden. (This despite inflation being higher today than it was when Trump took over last year.) But the AP-NORC poll is the latest to suggest that strategy won’t work. It shows 65% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for high prices more so than factors beyond his control. That number for Biden just before the 2022 midterm elections was much lower: 44%. Perhaps Trump’s party can still do OK in the upcoming midterms. But if it does, it will be despite historic dissatisfaction with the president on voters’ clear No. 1 issue.
