Baird was a passionate supporter of refugees and advocated on their behalf throughout his career.
While a Liberal MP, he opposed the Howard government’s mandatory detention of asylum seekers. After leaving office, he became a member of Kevin Rudd’s refugee resettlement advisory council.
In 2010, Baird criticised the reopening of Curtin detention centre in Western Australia to house asylum seekers.
“Don’t confuse treating people badly when they arrive with effective border control mechanisms, they are two different things,” he told the ABC.
“If we rely on treating asylum seekers badly in this country then there is something about us that we need to have a hard look at. I don’t believe that is the Australian way.”
Baird was also a regular feature of Manly’s Bold and Beautiful ocean swimming club. A member of the squad also confirmed his death on Friday.
On Thursday, the club’s organiser, Peter Anthony, wrote to members describing Baird as a “wonderful friend to so many of us”.

theguardian.com.title: Andy Burnham urged by Lib Dems to reveal all meetings with owners of Manchester City
theguardian.com.text:
Andy Burnham is facing calls from the Liberal Democrats to publish details of all his meetings with Manchester City’s owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), and declare all hospitality he has accepted at the Etihad Stadium.
The prime minister was widely criticised this week for saying he would be “really concerned” if ADUG were forced to sell City after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations, which led to Downing Street issuing two clarifications of his position on Thursday.
Burnham also praised ADUG’s investment in Manchester, having had close relations with the company, through which Sheikh Mansour bought City in 2008, during nine years as the mayor of Greater Manchester which ended when he returned to parliament this summer.
The Lib Dems’ spokesperson for culture, media and sport, Anna Sabine, told the Guardian that Burnham’s ties to ADUG should be scrutinised and is planning to write to Downing Street and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to demand details of their meetings.
“Football fans up and down the country deserve to know that the rules apply to everyone, however rich and powerful they are,” Sabine said. “When the prime minister leaps to the defence of a club’s owners within hours of a verdict, people are entitled to ask what their relationship is.
“Andy Burnham must come clean and publish details of every meeting and conversation he has had with City Football Group, Abu Dhabi United Group or UAE government representatives, going back to his time as mayor – and that includes any hospitality freebies received.”
Burnham, an Everton fan, has been pictured attending City games at the Etihad Stadium in hospitality areas.
The extent of that hospitality is unclear because under GMCA regulations the public disclosure of gifts is available for current office holders without the submission of a freedom of information request.
Burnham has not been to a City game since he became prime minister but has attended two Everton matches at Hill Dickinson Stadium, where he was accommodated in the directors’ box despite having a season ticket in the South Stand.
City confirmed on Friday that they had appealed against an independent commission’s verdict. They repeated their assessment that the verdict “contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe”.

theguardian.com.title: ‘We just want to be listened to’: student protests shut schools across France
theguardian.com.text:
As dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class.
“We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.”
“School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June.
“The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support.
The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by the thousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schools across the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week.
Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.
The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east.
Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”.
Outside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year.
“The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.”
On Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school, let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.”
Camille, 18, who said she wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.”
Farther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls.
Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special €1 meals for struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.”
He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re do nothing to remedy that.”

theguardian.com.title: Police divers find body of person missing after helicopter crash near LA
theguardian.com.text:
Police divers have found the body of a patient who went missing after a medical helicopter crashed into the Pacific Ocean off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, bringing the death toll to three while two other people were recovering from their injuries, the authorities said on Friday.
Divers with the Los Angeles county sheriff’s department found the victim’s body Thursday in the wreckage of the helicopter after searching more than 156 sq miles (404 sq km) over 23 hours, the Coast Guard said in a statement.
Relatives of the missing person told local TV network ABC7 that the woman was being transported from Catalina Island to the mainland for medical care after having an allergic reaction. They also said her 20-year-old son went with her in the helicopter to help as a language interpreter.
The helicopter with five people onboard went down shortly after takeoff and hit the water not far from the island, officials said. The cause is not clear and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. First responders pulled four people from the water on Wednesday night.
Robert Luna, the Los Angeles county sheriff, said authorities were not yet identifying the victims by name. But he described two of the people who died as the male pilot and a female nurse. He also said another medic and a fourth person, a man, were hospitalized. Luna said the helicopter wreckage was about 200ft (60m) deep in the water.
The helicopter’s operator, Reach Air Medical Services of Sacramento, confirmed that two of its crew members died and a third was recovering at a hospital. The company declined to provide more details.
A memorial service was held on the island to honor the victims.
The helicopter had landed on the island shortly after 7pm after a 24-minute flight from an airport in Oceanside, on the California coast between Los Angeles and San Diego, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
Janice Hahn, the Los Angeles county supervisor, said it was a terrible tragedy, adding: “The people who were on board dedicated their careers to saving lives. They are heroes.”

theguardian.com.title: Man shot by ICE in Texas has surgery to remove bullet lodged in his back
theguardian.com.text:
The Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot and wounded by a federal immigration agent in Texas last month had surgery on Thursday to remove the bullet that had been lodged in his back for nearly two weeks.
Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, had appeared in court in a wheelchair on Wednesday, wearing a sling on his arm. He remains in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to evade arrest.
Supporters and representatives had been lobbying for him to be given the chance of surgery, asserting that there was a risk he would lose feeling on the left side of his body because of the bullet being stuck so close to his spine.
He had been taken from a hospital where he was being treated after being shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin and put in detention at a facility about 140 miles away the same day.
The authorities said Garcés Pérez struck an officer with his side mirror on 20 September while trying to drive away after a traffic stop and questioning. The federal officer who shot Garcés Pérez, and who allegedly was hit by the side mirror of the car, was not wearing a body camera.
Garcés Pérez faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted on the assault charge. He was also facing deportation when he was stopped while driving on a DoorDash delivery in Austin last month, with some of the incident caught on bystander footage, including how ICE officers called an ambulance and then stood by as the wounded man sat in his car and then was given first aid by local police when they arrived.
The bullet was successfully removed during surgery, and Garcés Pérez is recovering in the custody of the US Marshals, said Fabiana Meléndez Ruiz, a spokesperson for his legal team.
His case has sparked outrage and protests in the Texas capital city against Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, including federal officers’ conduct. It was the latest shooting by ICE officers.
Garcés Pérez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and his car spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garcés Pérez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the officer fired his weapon.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

theguardian.com.title: Does Philadelphia’s ‘house of horrors’ hold the key to seven missing women?
theguardian.com.text:
A dilapidated house, burned out above the second story, may hold clues to dark tales and – potentially – the darkest of endings as the FBI and police in Philadelphia try to unpick what took place at 417 West Chew Avenue for more than three decades.
Last week, homicide investigators shifted their focus from examining an archive of a million photographs and film recovered from what is known locally as the “house of horrors” to excavating what is in or under the home of Raymond “RC” Horsch, a career criminal, local artist, author and snuff photographer who died last year aged 82, and his son Eugene, 44.
So far, at least seven missing women have been linked to the home in the Olney section of the city, originally a German American neighborhood but now largely African American, Hispanic and Asian. Investigators believe five are dead.
Fifty-eight women seen on film and in photographs recovered from the trash-strewn property have been identified. Of those, 25 have been located but not yet interviewed; 19 have spoken with detectives but declined to cooperate.
Investigators are faced with a difficult task: how to discern from images whether Horsch’s subjects are posing, and what is real and what is staged. Such is the grim nature of snuff photography and the murky exchanges that lie beneath. Investigators have said that the five women appear unconscious, lifeless or injured, but with no bodies the medical examiner cannot issue death certificates.
“We’re going slow and methodical,” a police source said. “Do we think people were killed in the house? Sure. It’s a tough investigation because the guy who had the house was a violent pornographer. Is it art or is it reality?”
Deputy police commissioner Frank Vanore said at a news conference on 10 September: “Some of this is play-acting. Some of it we believe could be real, but we’re not there yet.”
The five women who police believed to be dead are Blair Tonzelli, 35, missing since 2023; Nicole Fusaro and Maribel Fresses, both 27, who disappeared in 2018; Amy McHale, who disappeared in June 2016 and had been married to Horsch; and Gabrielle Amarando, 22, who disappeared in 2012.
Four miles from the Olney home lies Philadelphia’s Kensington neighborhood, an area notorious for its open-air drug use, prostitution and homelessness, and as a place where people simply disappear from life.
Many women in the community last week recalled some of those identified by investigators. One had connections to the Olney house – her driver’s license was registered there – but declined to discuss the case. Others said they recalled Horsch’s son, Eugene, currently in custody pending federal gun and drug charges, cruising the block in a black BMW. One remembered Fresses as an “Italian princess – sweet and kind”.
Ashley, making her way from a woman’s shelter with a plastic bag of candies, syringes, and a glass bowl for smoking fentanyl or meth, said bleakly: “A lot of girls go missing here. You get dope sick, it makes you crazy, and then you make bad decisions.”
Not all the women who passed through the Olney home were connected to Kensington. Media reports suggest that some met Horsch in Camden, New Jersey, 20 miles away. A woman from the area told ABC Philadelphia she had gone to the Olney home, blacked out from the drugs Raymond Horsch gave her, and woke up with him standing over her, taking pictures.
Police first raided the home in June after Eugene Horsch was stopped in a car in Philadelphia’s Old City neighborhood. Horsch was carrying fake ID indicating he was federal law enforcement and DEA agent. A female passenger was carrying Tonzelli’s identification.
Two handguns and approximately $8,000 worth of illegal drugs were found in the vehicle. According to court documents, Eugene Horsch allegedly said Tonzelli would “never be seen again”. A search of the home turned up an additional illegal firearm, a marijuana grow operation, a fake FBI badge and five urns containing cremated remains.
The arrest of the younger Horsch, who had not been charged in connection with the missing women, shone a spotlight on his father, who was never charged in connection with the disappearances of any of the five identified women. The city’s medical examiner’s office has advised that if images of at least three women recovered from the home “are authentic and have not been altered, the women depicted appear to be deceased”.
Court records show that Raymond Horsch was convicted in 2009 for attempting to lure a nine-year-old girl into his car in Kensington. “Come here, in my car, sexy girl,” Horsch said to her, according to an arrest report. Horsch was found guilty, sentenced to two and a half to five years in prison, and required to register as a sex offender.
But his lawyers sought a new trial and the case collapsed because the girl was too afraid to testify a second time, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer. Horsch’s conviction was expunged and the records placed under seal. A judge has ordered them to be preserved.
According to a 1985 psychological examination obtained by the Inquirer, Horsch was a manipulative criminal who was “consumed by anger … grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious, and excessively controlling”.
The profile was commissioned as part of a federal drug manufacturing case. Horsch fled the US with his second wife, Myroslawa Anna Ferkuniak. He was arrested in New Zealand, where he’d been living under the name of Stanley Stokowski, a real California chemist who had a Stanford doctorate.
According to the profile, he spoke in the third person, as if describing “events from someone else’s life”. Michael Yoder, a retired FBI special agent, told the outlet that, judging from the report, “I would say you have a potential serial killer on your hands.”
For a time, Horsch and his young son lived in Pennsylvania’s Berks county, where he opened a barbecue restaurant while also pursuing a career as a fetishistic or “snuff” photographer. In 2009, he was arrested after a marijuana grow operation was discovered in his basement, and he was sentenced to five years in prison.
Raymond Horsch had been offering cash and drugs to women in Kensington in exchange for participating in his violent pornographic films since the early 2000s. He also had access to to a crematorium connected to Kensington’s Garzone funeral home to photograph corpses. In 2007, the business was shut down for selling body parts on the black market.
Horsch wasn’t hiding his access to the morgue – a video exhibited at a “Transgressions” art show in 2014 featured a body being loaded into an incinerator. The exhibition asked visitors to consider if Horsch’s “often transgressive images can possibly be art? Or, as many critics and philosophers claim, are art and pornography completely and forever mutually exclusive?”
Horsch was not reticent about his obsession with women in addiction. He uploaded photos of his subjects to his website featuring women “imagining and acting their own deaths” juxtaposed with real photos of overdose victims. A handwritten note found in the home describes hurting people and makes reference to serial killer Ted Bundy.
Horsch’s films included a documentary, Whore!, and films including Deleted Scenes: A Serial Killer’s Video Journal and Slaves. He starred in and directed Lovers, which was produced by a feminist porn studio. He produced The Erotic Memoirs of a Male Chauvinist Pig, featuring Georgina Spelvin, the star of The Devil in Miss Jones.
He published a two-volume photo book called Eroto~ To the Prurient Interest, showing a woman he referred to as “Anna” in staged “deaths”. 2014’s Empathy included a chapter about dissolving a murdered woman’s body with chemicals.
The home is already a tourist attraction even as investigators still search for evidence. “It was creepy vibes. He’d be out front staring at women, or he’d be in his yard doing some kind of chemist stuff,” recalled Jessica Diaz, 37. A neighbor living opposite the home said he recalled young women coming and going from the home. On occasion, ambulances were called. “They need to tear that house down,” he opined.
With Raymond Horsch dead, and his son Eugene under investigation, it remains possible that no charges will be brought and the best the families of the missing can hope for is a police report. “We have a duty to those families who are all concerned about whether their loved one lost their lives in that house or maybe somewhere else,” said the Philadelphia police commissioner, Kevin Bethel.
But the story of Raymond Horsch is already entering the annals of Philadelphia horror lore. Edgar Allan Poe and Bram Stoker both wrote in the city, and it’s had serial murderers in the past. In the 1980s, Gary Heidnik, an inspiration for the fictional character Buffalo Bill in The Silence of the Lambs, imprisoned six vulnerable women in a pit in his basement with the goal of creating a “baby farm”.
Josh Hitchens, a writer and historian known locally as a prominent “purveyor of the macabre”, said that in each case, it was people preying on the vulnerable. “These are often not the people that law enforcement pays much attention to. That’s one of the horrifying things about what’s unfolding now – what Raymond Horsch was doing was apparently known and talked about within the community.”
Hitchens said Horsch is likely to become a point on the horror map of Philadelphia, achieving a measure of recognition in death that his films and writings failed to secure in his life.
“I hope that within that we’re not just talking about Raymond and Eugene Horsch, but the lives of the women are also remembered and given the respect they deserve.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘A persistent crisis’: the 16 children removed from an Ohio family are part of a statewide issue
theguardian.com.text:
In June 2025, Jody Walker stood in front of Ohio lawmakers at a senate finance committee meeting in Columbus. As the head of South Central Ohio Job and Family Services, he was desperate for help.
“I have been a county director since 1999, yet I have not seen such a challenging time in the child welfare system as I do today,” he said, “specifically in terms of the needs of our children.”
His agency, which oversees three rural counties in southern Ohio, frequently saw children sleeping at the organization’s office because they had no other safe place to go.
Twelve months later, Walker’s fears were realized right in his own backyard. On 30 June, 16 children were found in a dilapidated home in Hamden, a short drive from where Walker works. Several were found near death; two children were flown to a level one trauma medical facility, where one was placed in an intensive care unit, according to reports.
Gary Siders and Christina Siders, the children’s grandparents, and Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders, their parents, were charged with 16 counts of child endangerment. In August, Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders were additionally charged on separate counts of sexual battery and unlawful sexual conduct with a minor, who was not their own child. All four have pleaded not guilty to the charges.
The Siders case illustrates major shortcomings among Ohio’s political and administrative authorities when it comes to supporting the most at-risk in society, say experts.
“Our biggest challenge is a persistent crisis in identifying appropriate, affordable and accessible placements … Paid placement costs have increased 41% since 2020, far outpacing inflation, with the cost for residential and group home care skyrocketing by more than 65%,” said Angela Sausser of the Public Children Services Association of Ohio, which represents public children services agencies in the state.
“While the state share [of spending on children services] has been rising over the last eight years, from 10% to 20%, it still falls below the national average of 42%.”
Today, the family services department in Vinton county is drowning in the estimated $200 per child per day expense of caring for the 16 Siders children, who are now in foster care; six of the children are twins aged four or younger.
A rural region with fewer than 13,000 residents, Vinton county is the least populous county in Ohio. Property tax levies in the area fail to come close to covering the costs of caring for at-risk children, which for South Central Ohio Job and Family Services rose from less than $4m in 2015 to more than $10m in 2024.
In fact, the conditions facing the children were discovered by accident. Law enforcement went to the property to serve arrest warrants on Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders on charges unrelated to the neglect of their children.
“County leaders should not have to choose among services for vulnerable children, public safety, seniors and those with behavioral health needs or developmental disabilities,” said Sausser.
For more than 30 years, Republicans have broadly controlled governing and lawmaking in Ohio, regularly holding a supermajority in the state legislature. According to the Annie E Casey Foundation, a private philanthropic organization focusing on children’s needs, while the percentage of children in Ohio living in high-poverty areas has fallen in recent years, figures for child deaths, children without health insurance and children aged three and four who are not in school all have risen.
Financial disclosure information from the Siders family published by Los Angeles magazine found that Elizabeth Siders had no income and her husband’s salary amounted to $1,500 per month in 2021.
Ohio isn’t alone in struggling to fund care for vulnerable children.
Nationally, a swathe of cuts including supports such as food benefits for 1 million children are under way. For the 2027 federal budget, the Trump administration is proposing cuts to nutrition programs for women and children, home energy assistance for low-income families, a $6bn cut to the budget of the National Institutes of Health and the elimination of a federal preschool development grant program.
Data and research overwhelmingly show that children in states governed by Republican leadership face higher risk factors than those run by Democrats or members of both parties. The infant mortality rates in Tennessee, Mississippi and Arkansas are more than 50% higher than in states such as New York and California.
In Ohio, a case worker reported in 2020 that the Siders children suffered from high levels of lead; last year, Republican lawmakers in Ohio cut funding for a lead abatement program from $7.5m to $250,000 a year.
The office of Andy Wilson, Ohio’s Republican attorney general, declined to comment on questions from the Guardian asking, among other things, whether he believed the state of Ohio had failed the Siders children. Search warrant materials have been sealed by a judge, and a gag order has been issued by another, meaning attorneys for the accused and others involved, including law enforcement, cannot speak publicly on the matter.
Wilson has claimed that the adults in the Siders household “[w]ere pretty adept at keeping these kids out of sight and out of the eyes of investigators” and called the family members responsible for the abuse “pure evil”.
State authorities through the Ohio department of children and youth have initiated a review of the Siders case, “to determine how the county public children services agency followed federal and state requirements and to provide technical assistance on best practice”, said Jodi Norton Trimble of the Ohio DCY.
However, reports show that child and family services at the county and regional levels made significant efforts to highlight the conditions the Siders children faced.
When the family lived in neighboring Gallia county in 2020, a staff member from its department of jobs and family services visiting the children reported finding them living in desperate conditions, prompting court-ordered protective supervision for the children. But by May 2021, the supervision requirement was terminated and the family moved out of Gallia county.
The same year, school officials in Gallia county filed a complaint in a juvenile court reporting that several of the Siders children had become habitually truant.
But local authorities were unable to keep up with the family’s movements.
“I believe the school made contact with the appropriate school district where the family was living in West Virginia. However, before authorities could take action, the family moved again,” a representative of Gallia juvenile court said.
At 34 years old, Elizabeth Siders, the mother of all 16 children, was pregnant every 15 months. She was 15 years old when she was married in West Virginia, (before 2023, a child of any age in the state could legally be married with permission of a judge) and, shortly after, gave birth to her first child at the Holzer health system outside Gallipolis, Ohio. She would give birth to nine children at the facility, according to reports.
Her attorneys have called for a mental health evaluation to see whether she is competent to stand trial.
The Ohio department of children and youth report on the incident is expected to be completed by the end of the year, “but it must be conducted without interfering with the criminal investigations that are ongoing”, said Norton Trimble.

theguardian.com.title: Gordon Ramsay’s UK restaurants stay in red despite sales topping £100m
theguardian.com.text:
The UK arm of Gordon Ramsay’s restaurants empire remained in the red last year despite sales topping £100m for the first time after a string of openings in a London tower.
The celebrity chef’s UK business, which has 34 outlets including the Savoy Grill, Pétrus and several Lucky Cat restaurants, narrowed losses to £5.8m from £9.4m the year before. Sales rose 3% to almost £101m.
Andy Wenlock, the chief executive of Gordon Ramsay Restaurants, said that despite what the company called a “challenging macro environment” around the world, the group had begun 2026 “with strong momentum and clear priorities”. Those aims include improving profitability and “maintaining disciplined investment in our owned estate, and accelerating international growth through experienced partners”.
He said trading had been helped by the airing of the Netflix documentary Being Gordon Ramsay in February and the opening of the group’s 100th restaurant, at Bread Street Kitchen & Bar in Bishopsgate in the City of London. It is one of several restaurants on the upper levels of the 22 Bishopsgate tower.
“We remain positive about the UK market which is home for us,” he said. “Regionally and [in] London it is still full of opportunity, creativity and amazing talent.”
Globally, the company which operates 103 restaurants including the UK group, increased sales by 7% year on year to a record £151.8m as it wrapped in Ramsay’s US business, which is now co-owned with the investment group Lion Capital, and it reported “resilient” growth at established outlets.
Underlying group profits rose 12% to £14.4m as it opened a mix of owned restaurants and licensed partnerships including Gordon Ramsay Steak in Vancouver, Hell’s Kitchen in Ibiza and restaurants openings in the Middle East and Asia. However, the group – which does not include Ramsay’s TV production company – did not pay a dividend to shareholders.
“It has been an incredible year for the business and it’s testament to the dedication of the whole team to make it such a success,” Wenlock said.
“While 22 Bishopsgate has been the star performer, with five restaurant experiences in one venue, the strength of the performance of the group as a whole has been phenomenal, with openings across new and existing markets and a relentless focus on the guest experience throughout the brand portfolio.”
The group has signed new licence deals in the US and it said licensing partnerships, franchise and management agreements were expected to play an increasingly important role in growth.
Ramsay, who opened his first solo venture Gordon Ramsay at Royal Hospital Road in Chelsea in 1998, has struggled to make a profit at his empire for several years. However, the group has bounced back since the pandemic which brought Ramsay’s business operations to a halt and forced him to cut almost 300 jobs amid £12m in losses.

theguardian.com.title: Polanski says he does not need to win ‘50/50’ byelection to stay Green leader
theguardian.com.text:
Zack Polanski has said his authority as leader of the Green party of England and Wales does not depend on winning next week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection, amid suggestions the party’s popularity may have peaked.
Polanski, who is trying to take Keir Starmer’s former seat from Labour, described the contest as “probably 50/50 right now” and “really on a knife edge”.
Asked in an interview with the Guardian how much his position as leader depended on victory, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.”
He added that the election had ramifications for politics nationally but “not for my leadership”.
“I’ll be completely honest, it won’t surprise you to know that I want to win the seat,” Polanski said. “I think the seat is winnable, and I think it’s probably 50-50 right now. It’s really, really on a knife edge.”
Senior Green party figures privately fear defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership, amid concerns the party’s rapid rise in membership and polling has not translated into campaigning strength on the ground.
Attempts to concentrate resources on the byelection have caused internal friction, with the Guardian revealing last month that Polanski wanted the Greens’ annual conference postponed so the party could focus on the contest. That proposal was rejected by its executive.
Polanski, who has never been an MP, maintained there were “still advantages to being a leader outside Westminster”, while also arguing that entering parliament would offer another way of putting pressure on the Labour government.
The byelection has become an early test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can reclaim progressive voters who have moved towards the Greens, and the result may inform the government’s decisions over expanding North Sea oil and gas drilling.
“I see this election as high stakes for people in Holborn and St Pancras and high stakes for the climate crisis,” Polanski said. “We know that … a decision on [drilling projects Rosebank and Jackdaw] has been delayed until after this byelection, because Andy Burnham literally wants to see whether he can get away with drilling for new North Sea oil and gas.”
The Guardian has reported the Jackdaw decision is likely to be held until after the byelection, while a decision on Rosebank is still pending. Burnham has promised a more “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas than his predecessor, as the government balances its climate commitments against pressure over energy security and jobs.
Both projects already hold licences granted under the Conservatives, meaning approval by Labour would not amount to issuing new exploration licences.
Asked whether Burnham’s surge could win back younger and progressive voters from the Greens, Polanski said there were two possibilities. One was that Burnham “means what he’s saying right now” and would actually “implement action today and not tomorrow, and not after the next general election”. In this case, Polanski said, the country would improve as a result of pressure from the Greens and others.
The other, which Polanski called “the more likely scenario”, was that “what we’re getting is talk”. He said Burnham was “promising things after the next general election, but soon we’re going to have a budget that he’s already warning is going to be a difficult budget”.
In this case, he said, “more and more people will start to question why would you vote for the Labour party or get involved with the Labour party when the Green party has been growing for over a year now”.
He added: “You don’t have to accept the half-fat version. You can join the Green party and actually make sure we have the country that Andy Burnham’s talking about, but not taking the action on.”
Arguing that Labour’s climate policy had a gap between rhetoric and actions, Polanski asked: “Does Andy Burnham just not care about the climate crisis? It just feels like such a glaring gap in everything that he’s talked about, not just because of Rosebank and Jackdaw, but in the need to invest in renewables, the need for a clean green revolution, the need for new jobs, and it just feels like this vision is just not there.”
He added: “When are we going to see difficult choices for the super rich and the very, very wealthy? Instead, he’s talking about difficult choices for pensioners. So already, the action is not meeting his ‘hope’ rhetoric, and I think people are already starting to ask questions.”
Referring to arrests of Palestine Action supporters outside the Labour party conference, Polanski said: “Those people on the doorstep, they can see that Ed Miliband stood on stage and told many of us that we were right on Palestine, but just behind him, outside the conference hall, pensioners were still being dragged off, being arrested for holding signs up saying ‘I support Palestine Action’.”
Polanski is facing a separate test of his leadership at the Green party’s annual conference, where members are due to debate a deeply contentious motion declaring “Zionism is racism”.
Asked about criticism from senior Greens who believe he has failed to provide leadership over the issue, he said: “Leadership is about priorities, and this motion isn’t my priority. My priority is the cost of living. My priority is nationalising Thames Water. My priority is ending the genocide that’s happening in Gaza and freeing Palestine.”
Some Jewish Greens have raised concerns about what the motion could mean for their place within the party.
Asked whether he could guarantee that a Jewish member would not face disciplinary action simply for attending a synagogue that identified as Zionist, Polanski said: “I can guarantee that this motion has absolutely nothing to do with disciplinary action against anyone.”

theguardian.com.title: Minister denies UK faces diesel shortage after Trump threatens to ban exports
theguardian.com.text:
The government has sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting that the UK is not facing a diesel shortage after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
The transport minister Keir Mather said on Friday that the UK has a wide range of sources of the fuel and is in talks with other European countries over the potential release of emergency diesel stockpiles.
“I want to reassure people that they can still go to the pump and fill up with diesel because the supply we have to the UK is inherently resilient,” he said on ITV’s Good Morning Britain. “The flows of diesel into the UK come from a variety of sources, and that is resilient.
“The government’s obligation now is to work really closely with our partners [in Europe] and officials in the US administration to re-stress how important it is to have flows of diesel into the UK. People shouldn’t be concerned about shortages because of the inherent resilience that is built into that system.”
The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.
Earlier this week it emerged that the UK’s biggest refinery, Fawley in Hampshire, is set to shut for up to 10 weeks for planned maintenance. The UK had 18 refineries in the 1980s but now has only four.
On Thursday the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel supplies, after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring prices or face a US supply ban.
The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a record high on Friday, breaking the £2 mark for the first time, according to the motoring body the RAC.
“This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross,” said Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC. “The average price of a litre of diesel has risen to a record 200.01p and is showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery on to motorists.”
The government has extended the 5p cut in fuel duty until the end of the year. Earlier this week the RAC called on the government to extend the freeze into spring.
“We need to give people support where we can,” Mather said on GMB. “The government is not powerless. That is why we have a fuel duty freeze in place at the moment. The chancellor will set out the future of that at the budget, but is very aware of the impact that [high prices] are having on people.”
On Friday, Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said Europe was discussing the question of whether to release emergency reserves of diesel with all members of the International Energy Agency, not only the US.
“This is one of the opportunities that we have; we have used it before, and it is likely that we would use it again,” he told Euronews.

theguardian.com.title: OpenAI disclose another hack on government department in Australia
theguardian.com.text:
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has disclosed another unauthorised hack on a government department in Australia.
In June, an OpenAI agent hacked into a New South Wales state government department and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.
The breach, which comes weeks after news of a similar hack on a federal government department involving Medicare data, was not reported by the US based company until Thursday.
The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is now working with the state’s cyber security agency to investigate the breach.
The Australian Signals Directorate has also been informed of the hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service.
OpenAI told the NSW government that its agent had operated beyond its intended use and the statistics it obtained were not publicly available.
The company first became aware of the breach on Tuesday and conducted a 48 hours review to determine its scope before informing the NSW premier’s office.
“The results we reviewed do not show that the model retrieved any personal information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
This latest breach has added to calls for tougher regulation of AI companies and for bolstered cyber security defences.
“We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life,” Greens MP Abigail Boyd said.
Boyd said it was damning that the breach occurred in June but the government was not notified until this week.
“We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems,” Boyd said.
On Wednesday, the department of home affairs on Wednesday told federal departments to examine their older software and ensure cyber security was up to date.
The prime minister expressed his “extreme concern” about at an OpenAI agent hacking Australian Institute of Health and Welfare in June.
The Victorian Department of Health and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research were also compromised by an OpenAI agent.
An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools.

theguardian.com.title: Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding
theguardian.com.text:
Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding.
During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated.
This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure.
Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres.
The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

theguardian.com.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
theguardian.com.text:
On the eve of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.
Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.
But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the Pharaohs’ origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.
Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.
The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.
Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.
“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.
“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”
Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.
One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.
Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.
“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.
“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.
This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.
Monica Hanna, an Egyptologist at the American University in Cairo, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.
“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”
Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.
They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.
“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.
Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.
“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.
-
This article is published in collaboration with Egab

theguardian.com.title: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
theguardian.com.text:
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

theguardian.com.title: Activists plan legal action against police ban on entering security zone near Perth weapons expo
theguardian.com.text:
Activists and a Greens MP have threatened legal action after the Western Australia police banned at least 12 people entering a designated security area where the Land Forces weapons expo will be held in Perth from 6 October.
The police used special powers given to them by the WA government last month to ban the activists from entering the area surrounding the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre.
Two of the activists, 18-year-old Will Shanahan and 22-year-old Matilda Lane-Rose, said in a media conference held with the Greens MP Sophie McNeill on Friday they would take legal action if police and the police minister, Reece Whitby, did not revise the ban.
“We’ve sought legal advice, and we think that we have standing to pursue a judicial review into this decision,” said Lane-Rose, who works as a staffer for McNeill.
Lane-Rose told reporters the police called her on Thursday saying she had been placed on the exclusion list, despite having no plans to attend the protest against the expo, which is being organised by the WA Anti-War Collective.
The legislation used to ban her and 11 others, called the Land Forces (Special Powers) Bill 2026 was passed last month. It gives police expanded stop-and-search powers and the ability to ban people from entering a security zone that extends from the Elizabeth Quay bus port to the convention centre for 10 days.
Anyone who defies an exclusion order could face a maximum $36,000 fine and three years in prison.
The Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition event is held every two years and is Australia’s biggest weapons expo. The last event was held in 2024 in Melbourne, and attracted a large protest where police were accused of using excessive force.
Melbourne activists Violet Coco and Brad Homewood are among the 12 people issued an exclusion order by WA police.
The companies expected to exhibit at the expo are not listed on the Landforces website. Last month McNeill made public the list, which included an Australian subsidiary of Israel’s largest weapons company, Elbit Systems, and the state-owned company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
The two companies have been criticised by a former member of the UN commission of inquiry, Chris Sidoti, for being “key enablers of the Israel Defense Forces in its commission of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza over the last two years”.
Whitby said in response to the protesters comments: “We want Land Forces to be a safe and secure environment for attendees, workers, exhibitors, protestors and the wider community.
“These powers are preventative in nature and are intended to deter dangerous or disruptive behaviour before it occurs.
“Each excluded person has a demonstrated history of posing a serious threat to people and/or property.”
McNeill accused the government of using the legislation to target peaceful climate activists.
“They said that these powers were for people who had the propensity to commit violence, people who are a threat to the community,” she said.
“Instead, what we’ve seen is peaceful activists targeted … who didn’t even have any plans to be here in Perth next week. It’s outrageous.”
Shanahan, who recently moved to Newcastle from Perth, said they had not intended to attend the protest given they no longer lived in Western Australia, but now planned to do so, to defy the ban.
“I cannot sit and watch my home state be captured by global militarisation and be turned into an all-out police state,” Shanahan said.
Lane-Rose was fined $2,000 last year after pleading guilty with other Disrupt Burrup Hub activists to attempted trespass and criminal damage at the home of the then Woodside boss, Meg O’Neill, in 2023.
The WA police were approached for comment.

theguardian.com.title: Shoebridge pledges Greens members will ‘have a say’ in next leader – as it happened
theguardian.com.text:
Jeff Lapidos, who leads a branch of the Australian Services Union that represents Tax Office staff, has spent more than a decade fighting for better pay and conditions. He has also seen significant job cuts.
When asked about the Future Fund salaries, Lapidos said he did not believe in common salary levels across the public service. He said officials should instead be paid for the value of their work.
After inflation, the value of ATO employees’ salaries has fallen by 9.55% over the last 13 years. This is disgraceful exploitation by successive Coalition and Labor governments.
The ASU is campaigning for pay justice for all ATO staff. The prime minister deserves pay justice too. His office is vastly underpaid.
That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the week.
Before we go, let’s recap today’s top headlines:
“Visa hopping” international students, migration agents and lawyers trying to “game” the migration system will be targeted by the federal government, as Labor unveils a further crackdown.
NSW police believe two women who were allegedly assaulted and robbed during separate home invasions were targeted in premeditated attacks.
Online gaming services are failing to take enough action to prevent children being exposed to harmful content, a new report from the eSafety Commissioner has found. More on eSafety Commissioner, Julie Inman-Grant, who confirmed this morning “it’s probably time for new leadership” at the body after serving 10 years in the role.
A union leader campaigning for public servants to be paid more by the federal government says the prime minister is vastly underpaid. Earlier today, Guardian Australia reported on 11 public servants being paid more than $1m, which is significantly more than the prime minister’s base wage of $622,000.
The Coalition is railing against news the Australian Tax Office will no longer accept credit card payments from 20 November 2026.
Significant rainfall is expected to continue across much of Victoria, which has already been battered by storms and flash flooding.
Thanks for sticking around, have a lovely weekend!
Julian Hill backs Chris Minns’ comments on pace of migration
Assistant citizenship minister Julian Hill has backed comments made by the NSW premier, Chris Minns, about the pace of migration into Australia post-Covid.
During an appearance on Kylie Sandilands’ show, Minns said he believed “too many people came into the country in too short a space of time” in the years after Covid.
Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hill said he had not seen the specific comments but “broadly” agreed with them, while adding there were “a couple of nuanced points”.
Post-Covid – remember when the government was elected in 2022 coming out of Covid – we have the lowest unemployment in our country for over 50 years and employers right across the country, whether cafes, farmers, businesses were screaming out for warm human bodies who could be workers.
That was the big reason why net overseas migration peaked a bit too high post-Covid is the border reopened and fell a bit too slowly because fewer people were leaving.
A series of changes since coming to office to get net overseas migration down from a peak, it has fallen by about 50% and it needs to fall a bit further to get back to a sensible balance and give housing a chance to catch up.
Federal court justice Jonathan Beach heard evidence on Friday to help decide whether two separate cases against Medibank will be held jointly or as separate trials, AAP reports.
The health insurer is facing both a class action by affected customers and civil penalties brought by the privacy watchdog over the 2022 hack.
After Medibank declined to pay a ransom, personal data was leaked on the dark web under malicious file names, including boozy, STD and psycho.
A lawyer for the class action argued it was in the interests of justice to hear the cases together. Wendy Harris KC said.
The technical issues here overlap and intersect at multiple stages … in terms of the architecture of Medibank’s cybersecurity systems [and] the control deficiencies in them.
Neil Young KC, who is representing Medibank in both matters, called the class action a “total mess”, saying it went well beyond the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner’s case in its allegations of cybersecurity failures.
There are many new allegations of breach.
In order for us to address those new allegations, that’s going to require time.
Beach adjourned the matter until 16 October, in part to allow the class action party to consolidate its statement of claim.
Jeff Lapidos, who leads a branch of the Australian Services Union that represents Tax Office staff, has spent more than a decade fighting for better pay and conditions. He has also seen significant job cuts.
When asked about the Future Fund salaries, Lapidos said he did not believe in common salary levels across the public service. He said officials should instead be paid for the value of their work.
After inflation, the value of ATO employees’ salaries has fallen by 9.55% over the last 13 years. This is disgraceful exploitation by successive Coalition and Labor governments.
The ASU is campaigning for pay justice for all ATO staff. The prime minister deserves pay justice too. His office is vastly underpaid.
A big four bank is ending its relationship with its auditor of nearly six decades in the latest fallout from a whistleblower scandal, AAP reports.
KPMG has been ANZ’s auditor since 1969 and while the partners who worked on the audit have regularly rotated, the bank is looking for a new firm.
“A tenure of this length is no longer considered appropriate and has been under consideration by the board for some time,” ANZ said in a statement on Friday.
ANZ will begin a competitive tender process to select a new auditor beginning with the 2028-29 financial year.
The tender process will wind up in April and KPMG won’t be eligible to participate, the bank said. KPMG earned $21.4m for auditing and reviewing ANZ’s accounts in 2024-25, with its total fees, including non-audit services, coming to $29.6m for that financial year.
Shoebridge says party members will get input into leadership changes
Josh Butler
New Greens leader David Shoebridge says ordinary party members will have input into the next leadership decision, pledging a “conversation” to occur across branches and membership.
The Greens’ party room chooses its federal leader, which is the same as the Liberal and Nationals, but unlike Labor, which has a party room and membership vote. Shoebridge said this week, in announcing his leadership tilt, that he supported membership having a say; Mehreen Faruqi, who was unsuccessful in her leadership candidacy, said after the party room vote that she wanted members to have input.
In a social media video this afternoon, with the caption “your say on Greens leadership”, Shoebridge said: “You absolutely should have a say in the leadership for the Greens”.
“The good news is Steph [Hodgins-May] and I are gonna make this happen,” he said.
Shoebridge didn’t commit to any specific type of model, but said it would be “a conversation we’re going to have right across the Greens. Every state and territory, hundreds and hundreds of branches, thousands and thousands of members, because members want to be engaged in this.”
Shoebridge committed that the change would happen “before we make the next decision on the federal leadership”, which under Greens rules, happens after every federal election – so, in other words, in this term of parliament.
City of Yarra mayor cleared of assault allegation at election party
A prominent mayor has been cleared of punching a community activist who had gatecrashed his election after-party, Australian Associated Press reports.
The City of Yarra mayor Stephen Jolly, 64, said he was relieved to be acquitted of unlawful assault after Melbourne magistrate Jill Prior handed down her decision on Friday.
Jolly, whose council includes Carlton North, Collingwood and Richmond, fought the charge at a contested hearing, denying he intentionally struck activist Estella Burrows in the face on 1 November 2024.
Burrows and two other masked protesters had gatecrashed Jolly’s election after-party at a Collingwood venue, holding a banner and using a megaphone to accuse Jolly of abuse.
It was alleged Jolly punched Burrows to the face as he and other attendees forced the group to leave. The mayor denied intentionally hitting Burrows and separately argued he was acting in self-defence.
The magistrate on Friday determined Jolly did strike the left side of Burrows but she could not be satisfied he did so intentionally.
It was possible Jolly had been trying to disarm the group of their megaphone or he was reaching forward to move them away, the magistrate determined.
As a result, she found Jolly not guilty of the unlawful assault charge.
Outside court, Burrows told reporters she was disappointed but not surprised at the decision, claiming the justice system only worked in the favour of powerful white men.
Death row inmate Christa Pike survives two lethal injections in Tennessee – The Latest
The convicted murderer Christa Pike, sentenced to death, has survived two lethal injections and was taken to hospital.
Pike, 50, has spent three decades on death row after she was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. She would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
A last-minute appeal to stop the lethal injection was overturned by the supreme court, but the state governor, Bill Lee, has suspended executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year.
Lucy Hough speaks to the attorney and anti-capital punishment campaigner Clive Stafford Smith about the case in The Latest.

theguardian.com.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial: victim’s family cries as double murder trial hears triple-zero call
theguardian.com.text:
A triple-zero call made the morning Luke Davies and his partner Jesse Baird were allegedly murdered has been played to the court as photos of surfboard bags containing their bodies were released.
The recording was aired in the New South Wales supreme court on Friday during the double murder trial of former Sydney police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting Davies and Baird with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC told the court a call had been made to the emergency line from Davies’ phone at 9.50am on Friday 19 February 2024.
In the recording, movement can be heard before a muffled voice says “fuck off”. The call then drops out.
An attempt to call back goes straight to voicemail where Davies says: “Hi, you’ve reached Luke, please leave a message and I’ll get back to you.”
The Davies family cried in court as the audio played.
Police were sent to patrol the vicinity but were unable to pinpoint the exact address where the call originated.
Earlier on Friday, Ben Higginson, who served with the NSW police force criminal investigation team in Sydney, told the court about working with Lamarre-Condon the day before Davies and Baird were killed.
The two police officers had been working at a pro-Palestine protest on 18 February 2024 when Lamarre-Condon asked Higginson about work.
Higginson replied that it had been a “bit of a rough time” as he had been investigating the murder of Lilie James.
James, 21, was a water polo coach at St Andrews Cathedral school who was killed by Paul Thijssen in October 2023 days after the pair broke up.
CCTV captured Thijssen following James into the school’s gymnasium with a hammer before her body was found. He later killed himself at the Vaucluse cliffs.
Higginson became emotional when discussing the case with Lamarre-Condon, noting the crime had occurred at his old school, so it “hit home a bit more”, the court was told on Friday.
But when Lamarre-Condon asked about James’s murder he seemed “blase”, Higginson told the court.
“He thought Paul was stupid for doing it on CCTV,” the police investigator said.
Higginson told the court that Lamarre-Condon then asked if Thijssen hadn’t committed suicide “would he have gotten away with it?”
The investigator said police didn’t only rely on CCTV when examining a crime.
Higginson brought up the 2007 death of Matthew Leveson and told Lamarre-Condon he “could remember the CCTV of [Leveson’s] partner at Bunnings buying tarp, and he ended up burying him in the national park”.
Both police officers then spoke about how cash was more difficult to trace than bank cards and “what avenues detectives look at for suspicious deaths”, the court heard.
When Lamarre-Condon asked about phones, Higginson said he responded: “If you were to leave your phone at home and commit a murder, the phone would be showing up in the vicinity of your residence.”
The defence lawyer John Stratton SC said during his opening statement that Baird and Davies were fatally shot in “self-defence” after struggles with the policeman.
Lamarre-Condon immediately began cleaning up the scene because he “panicked”, the jury was told.
CCTV played to the on Thursday court showed Lamarre-Condon buying a second surfboard bag.
In the footage, the officer walks straight to the surfboard section of the Decathlon in Miranda Westfield, picks up a cover and pays in cash.
Baird’s housemate, known to the court under the pseudonym Sarah King, told the jury on Friday about returning home from work on the night of the alleged murders.
Their other housemate had sent a photo of red liquid, that she believed to be rusted water, underneath surfboard bags and tarp in their back courtyard and sent a photo to King.
King later looked at them, took a photo, and poked one of the bags.
Asked by the prosecution what it felt like, she said: “it just sounded like a tarp”.
Davies and Bairds’ bodies would be found days later in two surfboard covers near the fence line of a monastery in Bungonia.
The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

theguardian.com.title: Friday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfolded
theguardian.com.text:
Good morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers.
This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more.
This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world.
So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories
-
UK politics | Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.
-
Northern Ireland | Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”.
-
US news | Tennessee’s governor has suspended all executions in the state and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night.
-
AI | When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.
-
Europe news | A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned.
In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’
International leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury.
Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilot had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal. Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a “terror attack”. Two Israeli security sources later told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.
Saudi investigators detained the co-pilot upon landing and are cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to determine his reasons and potential affiliations. William Christou, a Beirut-based reporter with the Guardian, tells me: “They’re examining whether it’s a terror attack, whether it had any previous planning or prior direction, and if it could be a lone wolf attacker, who was perhaps motivated by anti-Israel hate, but wasn’t necessarily linked to any larger organisation or state.”
‘The story changed moment to moment’
William began drafting his initial report as soon as he woke up to news alerts about a potential hijacking. The Israeli government originally minimised the incident, describing it as a fight between pilots, while another early report suggested the plane had to land because of a fight between Ukrainian and Russian co-pilots.
“I was sifting through so much misinformation,” he says. “The story changed very quickly, and moment to moment.”
Back in the UK, Oliver Holmes was looking at flight trackers. Now based at Guardian HQ, Oliver has reported extensively across the Middle East. What I didn’t know until we spoke is that he once trained as a pilot, which has left him with an enduring interest in aerospace and aviation.
Flight tracking websites have transformed how we report in-air incidents, he tells me. “Before any government has made an announcement, these platforms can tell you something seriously wrong has happened.”
Flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft rapidly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes, just as it reached to the Saudi-Jordanian border. Oliver suggests that investigators will look at whether this sudden and ferocious plunge was why the plane eventually landed with part of its tail missing.
Oliver sent what he could interpret from the tracking data to his international desk editors, who asked him to work on a tick-tock piece – not, for once, a reference to social media, but an old-school print term for an article that sets out the hour-by-hour narrative of an unfolding news story.
“It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening,” says Oliver. Eventually there came a flood of footage purporting to show images from inside the plane – but was it real? Each clip that the Guardian incorporated into our reporting had to be verified, particularly given the potential for AI-generated fakes. (The Guardian’s head of photography Fiona Shields is fascinating here on how we assess AI images.)
‘Netanyahu was trying to present himself as Mr. Security’
But this wasn’t just an aviation disaster. “It was taking place in this hugely sensitive geopolitical situation,” says Oliver. “The plane landed in Saudi Arabia which does not officially have diplomatic relations with Israel.”
The budget airline itself, flydubai, had by now suspended all its flights to and from Israel, but warned against “premature speculation” while multiple governments, and Israeli officials in particular, were doing just that.
This incident has occurred at a moment of extreme instability across the region, with the strait of Hormuz still closed as a result of the US-Israel assault on Iran and the resurgence of conflict in Yemen. It is also weeks ahead of knife-edge Israeli elections, with polls showing Netanyahu’s current coalition unlikely to meet the threshold needed to form a government but no clear path to power for his rivals.
Just days ago, Netanyahu warned Israel faced an unspecified attack risk during the election period – an assertion greeted with cynicism by political opponents. The Israeli military subsequently confirmed they had no specific intelligence of an anticipated attack. “Most people interpreted that as Netanyahu trying to stir up his base by presenting himself as Mr. Security,” says William.
Nevertheless, Netanyahu’s supporters consider him vindicated.
